books.title: Nature Reuses and Recycles
books.art_why: Real-world recycling, organisms, and plastic waste can be photographed.

pages.text: Recycle, Reuse, or Trash? Clink! Bonk! Plunk! Those are the sounds of cans and bottles being tossed into the trash—or into the recycling bin. Items such as cans, bottles, and newspapers can be treated as trash, but they can be recycled instead. When you recycle something, the materials that make up the thing can be remade into a new thing. Word Wise The word recycle has two word parts: re - and cycle. The word part re- means “again.” The word cycle means to circle around. Just as a bicycle wheel circles around and around, recycled materials can move from your home to a recycling plant and back to your home again.
pages.brief: Cans, bottles, and newspapers sit between a trash can and a recycling bin, with one can and bottle falling in. Nearby, at a recycling plant, the same materials are shown being remade into new items, while a bicycle wheel suggests materials circling from home to plant and back.

pages.text: Recycling is different from reusing. When you reuse something, you keep it in the same form and do not have to break it down and remake it. When you reuse a bottle, you might fill it up with water again, but you don’t have to reuse something for its original purpose. When you reuse a soup can, you might keep pencils in it. When you reuse newspaper, you might use it to wrap birthday presents. After you are through reusing something, you can then recycle it or reuse it again!
pages.brief: A person refills a bottle with water, keeps pencils in an empty soup can, and wraps a birthday present in newspaper. Beside these reused objects, the same bottle, can, and newspaper appear again, ready to be reused once more or sent to be recycled.

pages.text: Nature Reuses and Recycles People are not the only ones who reuse and recycle. Nature does this, too, with organic materials. Organic materials are what living things are made of. By reusing and recycling organic materials in nature, living things adapt and survive. Take a tree. Every part of it can be used and reused in some way by other living things. Other plants, along with insects, birds, and other animals, have adapted to use parts of the tree to help them survive, too.
pages.brief: A large tree stands in a woodland, with insects, birds, and other animals around it. Sprouting plants grow near its roots. The tree’s leaves, branches, trunk, and roots are shown being used by other living things, showing how nature reuses and recycles organic materials so living things can adapt and survive.

pages.text: For instance, the original purpose of a tree’s leaves is to make food for the tree to survive. But a tree’s leaves also offer shade for sprouting plants. Birds line their nests with leaves. Sometimes squirrels reuse a bird’s nest for their own. Some insects make homes from dead leaves. That’s five uses for the same leaves! Trees are used in other ways, too. Owls make homes in the hollows of tree trunks. Beavers cut down trees and branches to make their homes. Some animals eat bark, leaves, and fruit from trees.
pages.brief: A tree’s leaves shade small sprouting plants, line a bird’s nest, and form a home for insects. A squirrel sits in an old bird’s nest, an owl looks out from a hollow trunk, and a beaver cuts a branch. Nearby animals eat bark, leaves, and fruit.

pages.text: Trees also provide valuable help to other living things when they die. Fallen trees become “nurse logs” that provide food and a protected place for new trees and other plants to grow. Dead trees provide a home for animals. They can also provide food and building materials for other organisms.
pages.brief: A fallen tree lies on the forest floor as a nurse log. New trees and other plants grow from its decaying wood, and small animals find shelter in and around the dead trunk. The log also provides food and building materials for other organisms in the woodland.

pages.text: Some Living Things Eat Dead Things When dead things decompose, they break down, rot, or decay. Imagine what would happen if nothing decomposed: dead plants and animals would just pile up! Lucky for us, several groups make sure that doesn’t happen. The first group that helps things decompose is made up of large scavengers. These are animals with backbones that feed on dead and decaying flesh. Large scavengers eat the dead flesh, then return the nutrients to nature through their waste. Nutrients give living things energy and help them grow.
pages.brief: Dead plants and an animal carcass decompose on the ground, breaking down and rotting. A large scavenger with a backbone feeds on the dead flesh, then its waste returns nutrients to the soil. Nearby, nutrients feed living plants, showing how decomposition keeps dead things from piling up.

pages.text: Many mammals scavenge. These include opossums, raccoons, dogs, cats, rodents, and skunks. Large mammals that hunt—such as hyenas, lions, and coyotes—also scavenge at times. Birds that scavenge include crows, ravens, and vultures. A second group of decomposers does not have backbones. It includes insects such as flies, beetles, and larvae (LAR-vee) that eat dead flesh. Earthworms eat dead leaves that fall to the ground or plants that have died and begun to rot. When earthworms eat dead plants, their bodies make waste. These bits of waste look like little blobs of soil, and in fact these blobs are rich food for plants. They contain many nutrients that plants need to develop and grow. Plants take up nutrients from the soil through their roots. The natural materials move in a circle from plants to worms and back to plants again.
pages.brief: An opossum, raccoon, coyote, crow, and vulture gather near dead flesh, while flies, beetles, and larvae feed on it too. An earthworm eats a dead leaf and leaves blobs of waste in the soil. Plant roots take up nutrients, showing materials moving from plants to worms and back.

pages.text: Earthworms at Work 1. The plant gets nutrients from the soil. 2. The plant dies. 3. The earthworm eats the dead plant parts. 4. The earthworm makes waste that mixes with the soil. 5. The waste has nutrients that feed a new plant, and the cycle begins again.
pages.brief: A plant takes nutrients from the soil, then dies. An earthworm eats the dead plant parts. The earthworm’s waste mixes with the soil, and that waste carries nutrients that feed a new plant. The new plant grows, beginning the same cycle again in the soil.

pages.text: The third important group is made up of microbes, such as bacteria and some fungi. These organisms are too small to see. They feed on many dead things, from fallen trees to the guts of dead animals. These organisms break down organic materials in things that have died. This process makes chemicals that can be used by other living things. Other fungi are big enough to see— mushrooms and toadstools, for instance— so these are not microbes. However, large or small, fungi break down dead things. Fungi are different from green plants, in part because they can’t make their own food. Instead, fungi feed on dead plants and animals, helping them decompose.
pages.brief: Microbes, bacteria, and fungi too small to see feed on fallen trees and dead animals, breaking down organic materials into chemicals other living things can use. Visible mushrooms and toadstools grow on decaying wood and dead plants, also helping them decompose.

pages.text: Fun Facts About Fungi More than 1 million different species of fungi live in our world. Mushrooms are some of the most visible—you might even spot some in your backyard after a big rain. Some are delicious. Some are deadly. Some fungi can cure disease, while others can cause it. Some can glow in the dark. And while some are too small to see, a fungus known as the honey mushroom may be the largest living thing on the planet. Believed to be 2,400 years old, it covers more than 8 square kilometers (2,000 acres).
pages.brief: Mushrooms appear in a backyard after rain. Some look delicious, some deadly, some glow in the dark, and some are used to cure or cause disease. A huge honey mushroom spreads across a forest floor, representing a fungus believed to be thousands of years old and the largest living thing.

pages.text: The Nutrient Cycle Decay can seem like an end, but it’s also a beginning. That’s because once something has rotted, or decomposed, the materials that made up that thing are free to make something else. All the things we need for life on Earth are already here. They’ve been here since Earth began. Those things change their shape and appearance, of course. But for life here to continue, this nutrient cycle must keep moving. Once a living thing has died, its nutrients must cycle back for some other living thing to use. Think of it this way: we are borrowing the things that make up our bodies. When we’re done, it’s time to give them back to the living. Decomposers help make that happen.
pages.brief: A dead leaf and dead animal decay on the forest floor. Their materials break down into soil, and a new plant grows from the nutrients. The scene shows decay as both an end and a beginning, with the materials of life changing shape and returning to living things through decomposers.

pages.text: The Problem with Plastic What doesn’t cycle through nature? Plastic. It simply piles up—in landfills, oceans, and just about everywhere else. The Great Pacific Garbage Patch is a floating landfill of garbage in Earth’s largest ocean. It’s twice the size of Texas and mostly made of plastic. Plastic takes a very long time to break down. Even when it does, plastic doesn’t enter into the nutrient cycle. It isn’t organic. All the more reason why humans, who create it, should also recycle it! Think of all the ways that living things use other living and dead things. You can see that nature does an awful lot of reusing and recycling. People should reuse and recycle as much as they can so they create less trash. But nature reuses or recycles every part of every living thing—it leaves no trash at all. We can learn a lot from nature.
pages.brief: Plastic bottles and bags pile up in a landfill and float in the ocean, forming a huge floating garbage patch. A recycling bin stands nearby. In contrast, a natural woodland scene shows dead leaves and plants returning to the soil, while people sort plastic to reuse and recycle it.

books.title: Barack Obama
books.art_why: A named famous person is the subject, so cartoon art fits.

pages.text: Introduction This is the story of Barack Obama, the first Black president. As a child, he sometimes felt as though he did not fit in. Barack learned about Black people who had become leaders in their communities. He developed a strong desire to help people living in low-income areas. Barack’s devotion to wanting to improve the world led him on the path to become the 44th president of the United States of America.
pages.brief: Barack Obama stands as the 44th president, with a younger Barack as a child nearby, looking unsure, and Black community leaders standing together in the background; people in a low-income area are shown working together.

pages.text: Growing Up Barack Obama Jr.—called Barry during his childhood—was born in 1961 in Hawaii. His mother was from the state of Kansas. His father was from the country of Kenya, in Africa. His parents met and married while they were students at the University of Hawaii. The marriage did not last. By the time Barry was four, his father had moved back to Kenya.
pages.brief: A cartoon baby Barry with his mother from Kansas and father from Kenya, the parents as students at the University of Hawaii, then the father leaving for Kenya while four-year-old Barry stays with his mother in Hawaii.

pages.text: Barry’s mother married a man from Indonesia when Barry was six. The family moved from Hawaii to Indonesia. Barry sometimes felt strange being so far from Hawaii. He felt he was not part of the community where he now lived. His parents were of different races and from different continents. Barry wondered who he was and where he belonged in the world. Barry’s Beginnings Do You Know? While Barry lived in Indonesia, he learned about the beautiful island country, its people, and its language. He also learned what life was like for people living in low-income areas. Many Indonesian families struggled each day just to have enough food to eat.
pages.brief: Six-year-old Barry stands in Indonesia with his mother and her Indonesian husband, looking unsure and far from home, while nearby Indonesian families in a low-income area struggle to find enough food; Barry wonders who he is and where he belongs.

pages.text: Barry’s mother taught him about races and cultural groups. She told him about slavery and the civil rights movement in the United States. Barry also learned about important Black people who helped to improve the world. Barry’s mother wanted him to be proud of his background. But Barry also learned that some people were ashamed of the color of their skin. And he learned about people who thought others were bad just because of their skin color or religion. It was a lot for a young boy to think about.
pages.brief: Barry sits with his mother as she teaches him about races, cultural groups, slavery, the civil rights movement, and important Black people who improved the world; he looks proud but also troubled while thinking about people judged by skin color or religion.

pages.text: Barry lived in Indonesia for four years. Then his mother decided to send Barry back to the United States. In 1971, when Barry was ten, he moved back to Hawaii. He lived with his grandparents and went to school. In Hawaii, Barry again felt like an outsider. He was one of only two Black students in his class. Some of his classmates made fun of his unusual name. Do You Know? In high school, Barry read books to help him work through his difficult feelings. He learned about important Black people who felt like outsiders but who had successfully found their way in the world. He was inspired by leaders who believed in peaceful social change.
pages.brief: Ten-year-old Barry arrives in Hawaii to live with his grandparents and attend school, where he is one of only two Black students and classmates tease his unusual name; later in high school he reads books about Black leaders who felt like outsiders and found their way.

pages.text: Finding His Way Barry graduated from high school in Hawaii. Then he went to college in Los Angeles. Barry started using his Kenyan name, Barack, which means “blessed.” He learned that he didn’t have to choose between his white and Black backgrounds. He was both. Barack wanted to learn how laws and government worked. He wanted to help change some of the unfair things he saw. Starting in 1981, he studied politics at a university in New York City. In 1983, he graduated from the university.
pages.brief: Barack, now using his Kenyan name, graduates from high school in Hawaii, then studies politics at a university in New York City from 1981 to 1983; he stands as a young man who embraces both his white and Black backgrounds and wants to change unfair laws.

pages.text: Barack Obama wanted to help people in communities. He wanted to involve people in creating better lives for themselves. He also wanted local laws changed so people would be treated fairly. Obama found a job and moved to Chicago in 1985. He led an organization that helped people living in low-income neighborhoods improve their lives. Do You Know? While Obama worked in Chicago, he helped many people. • He set up a job-training program for Black people who had lost their jobs when factories closed. • He helped call attention to asbestos, a dangerous material found in the walls of low-income housing. • His organization started a tutoring program to help young people who wanted to go to college. • He managed a program to sign up new voters. He encouraged people to get involved in politics and work for fairer laws.
pages.brief: In Chicago in 1985, Obama leads an organization helping people in low-income neighborhoods; he sets up job training for Black workers who lost factory jobs, points out dangerous asbestos in housing walls, starts a college tutoring program, and signs up new voters.

pages.text: Obama’s work in Chicago made him happy because he was helping people living in low-income areas. But he saw that to make lasting changes, he would need to learn how to change laws. By changing unfair laws, communities could improve the lives of their people. Do You Know? Before entering law school in 1988, Obama traveled to Kenya for the first time. His father had died six years earlier. But Barack met many relatives, including his grandmother. Obama entered a very good law school near Boston in 1988. He earned a law degree in 1991.
pages.brief: Obama visits Kenya for the first time before law school, meeting many relatives including his grandmother after his father’s death; then in 1988 he enters a very good law school near Boston and earns his law degree in 1991, determined to change unfair laws.

pages.text: After finishing law school, Obama moved back to Chicago. He worked for a law company. He met a lawyer named Michelle Robinson, and they became friends. Obama invited her along when he visited some of the people he had helped in the 1980s. Robinson was moved by Obama’s desire to help people and improve the world. They married in 1992.
pages.brief: Back in Chicago after law school, Obama works at a law company and meets lawyer Michelle Robinson; he invites her to visit people he helped in the 1980s, and she is moved by his desire to improve the world; they marry in 1992.

pages.text: Getting into Politics Obama had become a lawyer to help people. But he soon saw that helping people as a lawyer was slow. He decided that entering politics and changing laws would be a faster way to help. In 1996, he won a seat in his state’s senate. In 2004, he won a seat in the U.S. Senate.
pages.brief: Obama decides that changing laws through politics is a faster way to help people than working only as a lawyer; in 1996 he wins a seat in his state’s senate, and in 2004 he wins a seat in the U.S. Senate.

pages.text: “Change will not come if we wait for some other person or some other time. We are the ones we’ve been waiting for. We are the change that we seek.” —Barack Obama Obama gave a hopeful speech at a meeting of the Democratic Party in 2004. He asked all Americans to work together to help the United States become an even greater country. Obama’s words inspired many people. Some of them wanted Obama to run for president in 2008. They were inspired by Obama’s clear thinking and his respect for all people. They wanted a president who believed in peaceful ways to solve problems.
pages.brief: Obama gives a hopeful speech at a 2004 meeting of the Democratic Party, asking all Americans to work together; his words inspire people who admire his clear thinking and respect for all, and some hope he will run for president in 2008.

pages.text: Conclusion In November of 2008, Obama was elected the 44th president of the United States. He became the first Black president in the history of the country. Obama began his job as leader of the nation on January 20, 2009. He, his wife, and their two daughters moved into the White House. In October of that year, President Obama won the Nobel Peace Prize for helping to make the world a better place. In 2012, he was elected to a second term. As president, Obama made many important changes. He worked hard to help millions of Americans afford healthcare. He also worked hard to make peace with other countries. Barack Obama will inspire future leaders for generations to come.
pages.brief: In November 2008 Obama is elected the 44th president and first Black president; on January 20, 2009 he, his wife, and their two daughters move into the White House, and later he wins the Nobel Peace Prize, is elected to a second term, and works on healthcare and peace.

books.title: The Hard Stuff! All About Bones
books.art_why: Real bones, animals, and human bodies exist today, so photographs can show them.

pages.text: The Hard Stuff! All About Bones.
pages.brief: A human skeleton stands upright against a plain background, showing the hard bones of the head, ribs, arms, legs, hands, and feet. The skeleton is the central subject, with no other objects around it. It presents the body's bony framework as a whole.

pages.text: Body Shapers Lizards have one. Elephants have one. Even fish have one. You have one, too! What is it? A skeleton! Skeletons are the bones inside animals’ bodies. The skeleton is the frame that muscles and skin wrap around. Skeletons give all vertebrates, including humans, their shape. You can probably name many animals just by looking at their skeletons.
pages.brief: A lizard, an elephant, a fish, and a human are shown with their skeletons visible inside their bodies. The skeletons form frames that muscles and skin wrap around. Each animal's shape is outlined by its bones, making the skeleton the clear focus.

pages.text: The human skeleton has 206 bones, starting at the top with the skull and ending at the bottom with the toe bones. Many bones have muscles attached to them by tendons. These bones help us move. Some bones protect soft organs inside our bodies, such as the heart and brain. And many big bones have special areas in the center that make blood cells. Tissues called ligaments connect all the bones together to form the skeleton. To learn how bones work, let’s take a closer look at different areas of the body.
pages.brief: A full human skeleton is shown from skull to toe bones, with muscles attached to some bones by tendons. A heart and brain sit protected inside the body. Ligaments connect bones together, and a close view shows the center of a big bone making blood cells.

pages.text: Heads Up Think about the human forehead—the part of the face above the eyebrows. The forehead is hard because the skull, or cranium, is under the skin. The cranium is one set of bones in the body. It protects the brain, a very important and very soft organ. The cranium is like a crash helmet, but it is not as strong. For that reason, people should wear a helmet for sports such as biking and skating.
pages.brief: A child wears a helmet while biking, with a cutaway view of the forehead showing the hard skull, or cranium, beneath the skin. Inside the skull, a soft brain is protected. The helmet covers the head as an extra guard during sports.

pages.text: If you think about your head, your skull might seem to be one piece. In fact, the skull is made up of many bones. The bones join at special joints called sutures. Unlike other joints, the sutures cannot move much. The skull has twenty-two bones, not counting the six in the ears and one in the throat. Under the cheeks, it is possible to feel the cheekbones. The jaw is made up of two bones. Major Skull Bones.
pages.brief: A human skull is shown with many separate bones joined at sutures. A hand touches the cheekbone area beneath the cheek, and the lower jaw is visible as two bones. The skull's many joined parts form the head's bony structure.

pages.text: If you look at a skeleton, you might see something missing from its face—a nose. The part of the nose that sticks out is not bone. Your nose is made of a tissue called cartilage (CAR-tih-ledj). A nose can be touched and moved around. Cartilage can bend. Your bones cannot. You also have cartilage at the ends of bones. Cartilage keeps bones from rubbing against each other. Skeletons also have teeth, but teeth are not bones. Teeth are harder than bones. The outside of a tooth is made of enamel. Enamel is the hardest thing in the body.
pages.brief: A skeleton face is shown with no nose, while a human nose is made of bendable cartilage. A hand gently moves the nose. Nearby, cartilage sits at the ends of bones, and teeth are shown as harder than bone, with shiny enamel on the outside.

pages.text: Put Your Back into It The skull connects to the spinal column, or backbone. The first few parts of the spinal column start at the back of the neck. These bumps form your backbone and continue all the way to your hips. The bones in the back are called vertebrae (VER-teh-bray). Spinal Column The spinal column has two jobs. First, it protects the spinal cord, which runs through the vertebrae. The spinal cord is the place where the nerves meet to send information to the brain. The second job of the spinal column is to let bodies bend, twist, roll, and flip. The backbone is a chain of bones, not one solid bone. It is flexible and can move in many directions.
pages.brief: A human spinal column runs from the back of the neck to the hips, made of vertebrae and a spinal cord inside. A person bends, twists, rolls, and flips, showing how the chain of back bones is flexible and can move in many directions.

pages.text: The skull is not the only set of bones attached to the backbone. The ribs and pelvic bones are attached to it, too. The ribs protect the lungs and heart. The lungs and heart lie inside the ribs, which form the rib cage. If a person bangs on their chest, their lungs and heart don’t get crushed because the ribs form a strong wall around them. A rib cage has twelve bones on each side. Near the top of the spinal column are the shoulder blades and the collarbones. These bones make up the shoulders. Near the bottom of the spinal column, two hip bones make up the pelvis. On each side, a pelvic bone looks like a small bowl. That’s because it holds the intestines and other lower- body organs.
pages.brief: A rib cage wraps around the lungs and heart, with twelve ribs on each side. Shoulder blades and collarbones form the shoulders near the top of the spinal column. Near the bottom, two bowl-shaped pelvic bones hold the intestines and other lower-body organs.

pages.text: And Now the Limbs Arms and hands let people lift and hold things. Legs and feet help people move around. The bones inside the limbs help people do these actions. Arms each contain three bones. One bone is the upper-arm bone, attached at the top to the shoulder. Two bones make up the lower arm, between the elbow and the wrist. The wrist and hand together have more bones than any other part of the body—twenty-seven! That’s a total of fifty-four bones for both hands. Because wrists and hands have so many bones, they are flexible and precise. If they weren’t, people couldn’t do things like tying shoelaces or writing.
pages.brief: A human arm and hand skeleton are shown from shoulder to fingers, with the upper-arm bone, two lower-arm bones, and many wrist and hand bones. Beside them, hands tie shoelaces and write, showing how the many small bones make wrists and hands flexible and precise.

pages.text: The bones of the legs and feet are like the bones of the arms and hands. The top of the leg is one solid bone, called the thighbone. The bottom of the leg has two bones. Between the upper and lower parts of the leg is one more bone—the kneecap. The kneecap lies over the knee joint. It protects the tendons beneath it that let the leg bend. Like the hand, the foot contains many bones—twenty-six. That’s fifty-two bones for both feet. The ankle and heel of a foot have seven bones. The ball of a foot has five bones. The foot has fourteen toe bones— two for the big toe and three each for the other toes. Skin and tissue on the bottoms, or soles, of the feet protect the bones when people jump and run.
pages.brief: A human leg and foot skeleton are shown, with the thighbone, two lower-leg bones, and a kneecap over the knee joint. The foot has many bones, including ankle, heel, ball, and toe bones. A person jumps and runs while the soles of the feet protect the bones.

pages.text: Don’t Get Out of Joint Along with 206 bones, the adult human body has over 100 joints. Joints are the places where bones meet. Bones are hard and do not bend. We can bend and twist because bones connect at joints. Not all joints are the same. The joint where the upper-arm bone connects to the shoulder bone is a ball-and-socket joint. The connection between the upper-leg bone and the hip bone is another joint of this type. The top end of the upper-arm bone has a ball shape. This ball fits into a round hole, or socket, in the shoulder. The elbow joint and the knee joint are hinge joints. Hinge joints bend only one way. The joints between the vertebrae are swivel joints, which tilt and turn. The last type of joint is a suture, like those on the skull. Sutures connect bones but do not move much.
pages.brief: A human body shows different joints: a ball-shaped upper-arm bone fitting into a shoulder socket, a hip joint, hinge joints at the elbow and knee, and swivel joints between vertebrae. A skull shows suture joints that connect bones but move very little.

pages.text: Inside Your Bones Bones may feel hard and solid like rocks, but they are not. Bones are alive with millions of bone cells. Bone cells need oxygen and food, just like other cells. On the outside, a bone is hard and solid. This part is the compact bone. Below the compact bone is the spongy bone. Spongy bone has holes to keep the bones light so our muscles can lift them. Inside the spongy bone is bone marrow. The body uses bone marrow to make blood cells. About half a pound of bone marrow makes about 50 billion red blood cells every day!
pages.brief: A bone is shown in cross section, with a hard compact outside and spongy bone full of holes inside. Deep inside the spongy bone, bone marrow makes red blood cells. Millions of tiny bone cells are alive within the bone, needing oxygen and food like other cells.

pages.text: Keeping Bones Healthy Even though bones are strong, they can break if they are hit hard enough. Broken bones can be fixed. Healing a broken bone takes a little help from a doctor and a lot of help from bone cells. For a bone to heal correctly, the bone must be put back the way it was before the break. Doctors may move broken bones to put them back in place. They set a cast around the body part where the bone was broken. The cast keeps the body part from moving so the bone can heal. As soon as a bone breaks, bone cells begin repairing it. Holding the broken bone in place with a cast lets the bone cells do their job.
pages.brief: A doctor moves a broken bone back into place and sets a cast around the injured body part so it cannot move. Inside the break, bone cells work to repair the bone. The cast holds the bone steady while the cells do their job.

pages.text: Bones need to stay healthy to remain strong. Exercising regularly is the best way to keep bones in good working order. Eating a well-balanced diet helps the bone marrow produce healthy blood cells. Legumes (such as peas or pinto beans), other vegetables, and fruits are good for bones. Foods rich in calcium, such as dairy products and fortified soy milk, rice milk, and orange juice, can also help bones grow. Bones give a body its shape, and they also give it much more. They allow the body to move, sit, stand, and write. Human bodies wouldn’t be the same without bones!
pages.brief: A person exercises and eats a balanced meal with legumes such as peas and pinto beans, vegetables, fruits, dairy, fortified soy milk, rice milk, and orange juice. The foods and activity support strong bones that let a body move, sit, stand, and write.

books.title: Wonders of Nature
books.art_why: Real animals and natural places can be photographed.

pages.text: Introduction The world is full of strange and interesting animals. Some animals look unusual or have special abilities. Let’s look at some of these strange animals and learn what makes them wonders of nature. Archerfish An archerfish squirts drops of water at an insect or spider to knock it off a leaf that hangs over the water. The archerfish forms a tube with its tongue and the roof of its mouth and then shoots drops of water through the tube. When a bug falls into the water, the archerfish eats it. Because the archerfish has a flat body, it can swim right under its prey and get into position without being noticed. Sometimes an archerfish leaps out of the water to catch a bug instead of squirting water at it.
pages.brief: An archerfish swims in water beneath a leaf hanging over the surface, forming a tube with its tongue and mouth roof to squirt drops at an insect or spider on the leaf. Its flat body is positioned under the prey; another archerfish leaps from the water to catch a bug.

pages.text: Trap-Door Spider A trap-door spider lives in a sticky underground tunnel with a hidden door. The spider’s body produces silk, which it mixes with dirt to make the door. The silk in the door helps keep water out of the spider’s tunnel when it rains. When an insect passes close to the door, the trap-door spider senses its movements and jumps out to grab it. Female trap-door spiders stay near their tunnels for their entire lives. Their offspring leave to build their own tunnels nearby.
pages.brief: A trap-door spider waits in a sticky underground tunnel with a hidden door made of silk and dirt. When an insect passes close, the spider senses movement and jumps out to grab it. A female stays near her tunnel, while offspring build their own tunnels nearby.

pages.text: Beaver Beavers chew through tree trunks with their sharp teeth. Beavers use tree trunks, branches, mud, clay, and stones to build dams in rivers and streams. The dams create ponds where beavers build their homes, which are called lodges. By building dams, beavers create wetlands, which are habitats for other mammals as well as for birds, fish, turtles, and frogs. Wetlands protect the environment by preventing erosion, soaking up floodwater, and acting as filters to clean water.
pages.brief: A beaver chews through a tree trunk with sharp teeth, then uses trunks, branches, mud, clay, and stones to build a dam across a river or stream. The dam creates a pond where the beaver’s lodge stands. Other birds, fish, turtles, and frogs live in the wetland the dam creates.

pages.text: Three-Wattled Bell Bird The three-wattled bell bird lives in Central America. Its call sounds like a large, heavy bell ringing. Female three-wattled bell birds are green, and males are brown with white heads. Three long, pointed flaps of skin called wattles grow from the male’s beak. The bell bird scares away enemies with its loud call and by shaking its wattles. The bell birds’ favorite food is the wild avocado. Bell birds migrate to different elevations because avocados ripen at different times of year at different heights in the mountains.
pages.brief: In a Central American forest, a male three-wattled bell bird with a brown body, white head, and three long pointed wattles on his beak calls loudly and shakes the wattles. A green female bell bird sits nearby near wild avocados growing at different heights in the mountains.

pages.text: Bower Bird Bower birds live in Australia and New Guinea. To attract female birds, male bower birds spend up to ten months building tall piles of twigs and branches around the bases of trees. They decorate these piles, called bowers, with shells, feathers, flowers, and fruit. Sometimes they even paint the walls with plant juice. Bower birds have also been known to use film cases, toothbrushes, and other objects made by people as part of their decorations. When the male birds finish decorating, the female birds choose the bowers they like best.
pages.brief: In Australia or New Guinea, a male bower bird builds a tall pile of twigs and branches around the base of a tree. He decorates the bower with shells, feathers, flowers, and fruit, and may paint the walls with plant juice. A female bird looks at the decorated bower.

pages.text: Chameleon Chameleons are lizards that can change their skin color to blend in with their surroundings. They can even change color to show how they feel. Chameleons catch insects with their long tongues, which can be twice as long as their bodies. Chameleons can point each of their eyes in a different direction at the same time to help them see all around them. When they spot an insect they want to eat, chameleons focus both of their eyes forward to help them aim their tongues.
pages.brief: A chameleon changes its skin color to blend with its surroundings and to show how it feels. Its two eyes point in different directions while it watches for insects. When it spots one, both eyes focus forward and its long tongue shoots out to catch the insect.

pages.text: Flying Dragon Flying dragons are small lizards that can glide through the air, usually from tree to tree, by opening folds of skin on the sides of their bodies like wings. The wings are brightly colored and have spots and stripes on them. Flying dragons use their sticky tongues to catch and eat insects, mainly ants and termites. They can glide long distances and can even turn around in the air to land on the same tree they took off from.
pages.brief: A small flying dragon lizard opens folds of skin on the sides of its body like brightly colored wings with spots and stripes, gliding from one tree to another. It can turn in the air and land on the same tree it left. It uses a sticky tongue to catch ants and termites.

pages.text: Leaf Insect Leaf insects live in hot places. Their bodies, wings, and legs look like leaves, which allows them to blend in with real leaves on trees. Their leaf-shaped bodies sometimes appear to have damage from insects eating them, but the markings are just camouflage. Leaf insects will even move back and forth to look like leaves swaying in the breeze. Leaf-insect eggs look like seeds, which helps to fool predators that eat eggs. The eggs can take more than a year to hatch. Baby leaf insects are red, but when they start eating leaves, they turn green.
pages.brief: A leaf insect rests among real leaves in a hot place, its leaf-shaped body, wings, and legs blending in. Markings on its body look like damage from insects eating leaves, and it sways back and forth like a leaf in the breeze. Seed-like eggs and a red baby are nearby.

pages.text: Leaf-Rolling Weevil In the summer, the female leaf-rolling weevil rolls a leaf into a cone shape. She takes up to two hours getting the leaf just right. She stops every couple of turns to bite wedges and add folds to help hold the cone together. When finished, she lays her eggs inside the cone and then closes the open end. When the leaf falls in autumn, it carries the eggs with it. The leaf hides and protects the eggs until they hatch. When the larvae hatch, they eat the dead leaf.
pages.brief: A female leaf-rolling weevil rolls a leaf into a cone shape in summer. She stops every couple of turns to bite wedges and add folds that hold the cone together. When the cone is finished, she lays her eggs inside and closes the open end. In autumn the leaf falls with the eggs.

pages.text: Praying Mantis The praying mantis often holds its front legs in a praying position. Mantises hide on plants to catch their food. Some praying mantises are green to blend in with leaves, while others that live in the desert are the color of sand. The praying mantis is carnivorous and eats many types of insects as well as small frogs, lizards, and mice. A praying mantis can even catch and eat small birds such as hummingbirds. A mantis has five eyes and can turn its head to look directly behind its body. Its two large eyes can see shapes and colors, and its three small ones just sense light and dark.
pages.brief: A praying mantis hides on a plant with its front legs held in a praying position. It is green to blend with leaves. Its head turns to look directly behind its body. Two large eyes see shapes and colors, and three small eyes sense light and dark.

pages.text: Mole Moles burrow underground to find and eat earthworms. They also eat beetles, slugs, and snails. Moles have big appetites and can eat their own body weight’s worth of food in a single day! After digging many interconnecting tunnels that form a maze, a mole builds its nest deep inside. Because its fur points up, a mole can move backward and forward in a tunnel without getting dirt trapped in its coat. Moles have tiny eyes, but they are not blind.
pages.brief: A mole burrows underground through a maze of interconnecting tunnels, searching for earthworms, beetles, slugs, and snails. Deep inside, it builds a nest. Its fur points up, so the mole can move backward and forward without trapping dirt in its coat. It has tiny eyes but is not blind.

pages.text: Sea Dragon Sea dragons are small fish that are related to sea horses. Their bodies have many parts that look like the stems and leaves of seaweed. They blend in with ocean plants, which helps them catch food and hide from enemies. The female lays many bright pink eggs on the male sea dragon’s tail, and the male carries the eggs until they hatch. Sea dragons don’t use their “leaves” to swim. Instead, they use small, clear fins on their necks and backs that are very hard to see. Conclusion Interesting animals come in many shapes and sizes. Their special looks and abilities help all these wonders of nature to survive.
pages.brief: A sea dragon, a small fish related to sea horses, swims among ocean plants that match the seaweed-like stems and leaves on its body. Small, clear fins on its neck and back move it through the water. Bright pink eggs are attached to the male sea dragon’s tail, where he carries them until they hatch.

books.title: Glow-in-the-Dark Animals
books.art_why: The keyword check points to drawing for this book.

pages.text: Glow-in-the-Dark Animals.
pages.brief: A dark nighttime scene with small points of light glowing in a night landscape and a dark ocean below, suggesting the book’s theme of living light in animals. The cover-like image hints at creatures that shine in darkness, with no single species shown.

pages.text: Living Light Some animals carry their own light— insects on land flash in the night, and fish and other sea creatures glow. These glowing animals make their own light. They are bioluminescent (BY-oh-loo-mih-NEH-sent). This long word means “life glowing.” The first part, bio, comes from a Greek word that means “life.” The second part, luminescent, comes from a Latin word that means “glowing.”
pages.brief: At night, several insects flash bright signals over dark land while fish and other sea creatures glow with soft light in deep ocean water. The scene shows animals carrying their own living light in two different habitats.

pages.text: Reasons to Glow Animals flash and glow to help them survive on land and in the sea. Their lights can be red, yellow, green, or blue. They use their lights to signal, hunt, and hide. They also use them to call for help and to fool their enemies. Glowing helps them survive. Most kinds of glowing animals live in the sea—very few live on land. You may have seen one of these glowing land animals on a warm summer evening. It’s the firefly, a kind of beetle. Fireflies produce the glow in their abdomen, the hind part of their bodies. The light is like a tiny flashlight switching on and off. This flashing is a signal that helps these beetles communicate and find each other.
pages.brief: On a warm summer evening, a firefly beetle rests on a leaf, its abdomen glowing like a tiny flashlight switching on and off. Other distant fireflies answer with flashes. The scene shows land animals using light to signal and find each other.

pages.text: Some glowing sea animals use their light to hunt. The anglerfish has a stalk on its head that acts like a fishing rod. The tip of the stalk has a glowing white light that attracts small ocean fish. As the anglerfish moves its “lure” back and forth in water, the small fish come close to investigate. Then the anglerfish swallows them whole in one big gulp.
pages.brief: Deep in dark ocean water, an anglerfish hovers with a long stalk on its head and a glowing white tip. Small fish swim close to investigate the moving lure. The anglerfish opens its large mouth, ready to swallow them whole in one gulp.

pages.text: Other animals use their glow to hide from predators —animals that want to eat them. Some squid squirt chemicals into the ocean water to make a glowing cloud. This glow hides the squid so the predator can’t find it. Then the squid escapes.
pages.brief: A squid releases a cloud of glowing chemicals into dark ocean water, creating a bright haze around its body. A larger predator swims nearby, unable to see the squid through the glow. The squid slips away as the glowing cloud spreads.

pages.text: Krill are glowing sea animals that look like tiny shrimp. They use their glow to keep from becoming the prey of fish and other ocean animals that want to eat them. Millions of krill use their lights to signal each other. The signals help them gather together in huge groups. These glowing, swirling swarms confuse the whales, sea lions, and fish that all rely on krill for food.
pages.brief: Millions of tiny krill, looking like small shrimp, glow and signal to one another in dark ocean water. They gather into a huge swirling swarm. A whale, sea lions, and fish swim nearby, confused by the glowing mass of krill.

pages.text: Some sea animals use their glow to fool predators that are swimming around below them. Their glowing light looks similar to the moonlight or sunlight that shines down into the ocean. The glow allows these animals to blend in against the bright surface of the water and makes it hard for predators to see them from below. The belly of the cookie-cutter shark glows with a pale blue-green color. This glow matches the sunlit water above the swimming shark. The blue-green glow camouflages, or hides, the shark. The shark also has a small, dark patch on its belly that does not glow. This dark patch tricks other fish because it looks like the shadow of a small fish. When a bigger fish comes near to catch it, the cookie-cutter shark attacks and eats the fish.
pages.brief: A cookie-cutter shark swims below in dark water, its pale blue-green belly glowing to match the sunlit surface above. A small dark patch on its belly looks like a fish shadow. A larger fish comes near to catch it, and the shark turns to attack.

pages.text: Chemical Reaction to Produce Light The Science Behind the Glow What makes these animals glow? Bioluminescent animals have two special chemicals in their bodies: luciferin and luciferase. When these chemicals mix with oxygen, they produce light. This chemically created light is different from the light that lightbulbs make. You would not touch a lightbulb that’s switched on—you might burn yourself. That’s because an electric lightbulb generates lots of heat as well as light. But the glow that animals make would not hurt you because it’s a cool glow. A glowing animal gives off very little heat.
pages.brief: Inside a glowing animal’s body, two chemicals mix with oxygen and produce a soft light. The scene compares the cool animal glow with a hot switched-on lightbulb, showing that the animal’s light gives off very little heat.

pages.text: How do glowing animals turn their glow on and off? Some scientists believe the secret is oxygen. They think that oxygen fuels the glow, and they believe that animals can turn their glow on or off by turning the supply of oxygen up or down. Other scientists have a different idea. They think that a tiny molecule in the animal’s body acts like a switch to turn the lights on and off. No one knows for sure.
pages.brief: A glowing animal is shown with a supply of oxygen and a tiny molecule inside its body. Scientists imagine two ideas for turning the glow on and off: oxygen rising and falling, or a molecule acting like a switch.

pages.text: Blink your eye. That’s how quickly some animals flash. Now take your time and count to ten. That’s how slowly some animals flash. And some animals glow for a long, long time without stopping. The glow from ocean animals comes in several different colors. Animals in the oceans glow mostly blue or green, but some glow red. Glowing land animals most often give off a green or yellow light.
pages.brief: A glowing ocean animal flashes in an instant, another glows slowly through a count to ten, and a third shines steadily for a long time. Nearby, ocean animals glow blue, green, and red, while land animals glow green or yellow.

pages.text: Three Ways to Glow Some bioluminescent animals make their light inside their body—the chemicals and oxygen are mixed inside them. Some jellyfish produce enough light to make their whole body glow from the inside. Others make only parts of their body glow.
pages.brief: A jellyfish floats in dark water, its whole body glowing from the inside. Other bioluminescent animals are shown with only parts of their bodies lit. The scene shows animals that make light inside their bodies by mixing chemicals and oxygen.

pages.text: Other animals produce their glow outside their bodies. They squirt the chemicals into the seawater. Then the chemicals mix with the oxygen in the water. That’s how some shrimp can spit out a glowing cloud. The shining blue cloud scares predators, and the shrimp swims away.
pages.brief: A small shrimp squirts glowing chemicals into seawater, and the chemicals mix with oxygen to form a shining blue cloud. A predator nearby is scared by the bright cloud. The shrimp swims away into the dark ocean.

pages.text: A few glowing animals do not make their own light—they borrow it. They use the glow of tiny animals called bacteria. The flashlight fish stores about a billion glowing bacteria inside a pouch beneath each eye. Sometimes the flashlight fish looks as if it’s blinking. That’s when the fish rolls the pouches up and down to turn the light on and off. Now you see it, now you don’t.
pages.brief: A flashlight fish swims in dark water with a glowing pouch beneath each eye. Inside the pouches are tiny glowing bacteria that the fish borrows. The fish rolls the pouches up and down, making the light appear and disappear like a blink.

pages.text: Ocean Light Zones Habitats of Glowing Animals Bioluminescent sea animals live in all of Earth’s oceans. Some live near the surface. But most glowing animals live deeper down, from about 200 meters (656 ft) to about 1,000 meters (3,281 ft). Scientists call this area the twilight zone. Sunlight in this middle part of the ocean is a dim blue-green color. Most of the glowing animals in the twilight zone produce a matching blue-green light.
pages.brief: In the ocean’s twilight zone, dim blue-green sunlight filters down through deep water. Glowing sea animals swim at different depths, most between about 200 and 1,000 meters. Their blue-green light matches the faint sunlight around them.

pages.text: Other glowing sea animals live even deeper down, at the very bottom of the ocean. No sunlight reaches this deep. All the animals that live at this depth are bioluminescent, and they provide the only light in this part of the salty ocean. Only a few kinds of glowing animals make their home on land. Among them are fireflies, glowworms, and the two-colored railroad worm.
pages.brief: At the very bottom of the ocean, no sunlight reaches, and glowing animals provide the only light in the dark water. On land, fireflies, glowworms, and a two-colored railroad worm are shown as the few glowing land animals.

pages.text: More to Know and Explore Scientists use glowing animals to learn more about nature. They study the way that small glowing animals move through water. Watching these tiny animals helps them learn how larger animals move through water. Scientists also use animal bioluminescence to learn more about diseases, such as cancer.
pages.brief: Scientists observe tiny glowing animals moving through water, using what they see to understand how larger animals move. In their research, they also study animal bioluminescence to learn more about diseases such as cancer. The scene shows careful scientific study of living light.

pages.text: Oceans cover about seventy percent of Earth’s surface. As a result, oceans are the largest habitat on Earth. When scientists explore new parts of oceans, they discover new kinds of animals. In 2009, scientists found a new kind of glowing animal, a swimming worm. They call it a green bomber. To escape from enemies, green bombers release little balloons of skin filled with a fluid that glows green. The glowing skin confuses enemies, which allows the green bombers to swim away. As scientists explore more parts of Earth’s oceans, they hope to discover more strange new animals that glow in the dark.
pages.brief: Deep in the ocean, a newly found green bomber worm swims away from an enemy. It releases little balloons of skin filled with a fluid that glows green. The glowing cloud confuses the enemy. Scientists explore more ocean areas, hoping to find other strange glowing animals.

books.title: Martin Luther King, Jr.
books.art_why: The book is about a named famous person, Martin Luther King Jr.

pages.text: Martin Luther King, Jr.
pages.brief: A respectful portrait of Martin Luther King Jr. He stands facing the reader with a calm, serious expression, wearing a suit. The background is simple and uncluttered, keeping attention on him as the book’s subject.

pages.text: Growing Up in the South Each January, people in the United States celebrate Martin Luther King Day. We honor a great leader who fought for the equality of all people. Who was this man? Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. was born on January 15, 1929. His father was a minister, and his mother was a teacher. In the South, where King grew up, white leaders created unfair laws known as Jim Crow laws. These laws robbed Black people of many rights. They also kept Black people and white people segregated, or separated.
pages.brief: A young Martin Luther King Jr. stands with his father, a minister, and his mother, a teacher in the South. A January scene shows people celebrating Martin Luther King Day and honoring the leader. Nearby, separate entrances and waiting areas suggest unfair Jim Crow laws.

pages.text: Many places, such as schools, bathrooms, parks, and bus and train waiting rooms, were segregated. Often, the places for Black people were not as nice or clean as those for white people. Black people also couldn’t live in white neighborhoods or marry a white person. They couldn’t have certain jobs and were paid less than white workers. As King grew up, he saw how these laws hurt Black people. He wanted to help Black people gain full equality. Martin Luther King Jr.
pages.brief: As a boy, Martin Luther King Jr. sees segregated schools, bathrooms, parks, and bus and train waiting rooms. The places for Black people look worn and less clean than those for white people. He also sees Black workers paid less. His face shows he wants full equality.

pages.text: King Goes to School King was a good student. At the age of fifteen, he started college in Atlanta, Georgia. He decided to become a minister like his father. King moved north to study religion. While there, King learned about Mohandas Gandhi, a leader in India. Gandhi believed in using peaceful protest to help people. King decided that he would use nonviolence, too. After King finished school, he and his wife moved to Montgomery, Alabama. He became a minister there. Coretta Scott King King’s wife, Coretta Scott King, was an important leader. After her husband was killed in 1968, she started a center in Atlanta to train people in how to protest peacefully. She also helped make her husband’s birthday a holiday in the 1980s. Mrs. King spent the rest of her life traveling around the world and supporting human rights. She died in January 2006.
pages.brief: A young Martin Luther King Jr. studies at college in Atlanta, then learns about Gandhi’s peaceful protests. He and his wife, Coretta Scott King, move to Montgomery, Alabama, where he becomes a minister. In a side scene, Coretta leads a center in Atlanta and travels to support human rights.

pages.text: The Montgomery Bus Boycott In May 1954, the U.S. Supreme Court said that schools could no longer be segregated by race. Black people hoped this would lead to the desegregation of other places. Many white people in the South supported segregation, though. In December 1955, a Black woman named Rosa Parks was riding home on a city bus in Montgomery. By law, Black people had to sit at the back of the bus. They were expected to give up their seat to a white person if asked. Parks knew this was unfair. When a white man asked for her seat, she wouldn’t move. The police arrested her. Martin Luther King Jr.
pages.brief: Rosa Parks sits near the back of a Montgomery city bus in December 1955. A white man asks for her seat. She stays seated, refusing to move. Police officers stand nearby and arrest her. Other passengers watch in the segregated bus.

pages.text: Black people in Montgomery were upset about Parks’s arrest. They called for a boycott to protest segregation on city buses. They started an organization to lead the protest and put King in charge. Most Montgomery city bus riders were Black. The city lost a lot of money during the boycott. Still, white city leaders refused to listen to the protestors.
pages.brief: Black community members in Montgomery meet and organize a bus boycott after Rosa Parks’s arrest. They put Martin Luther King Jr. in charge of the protest organization. Empty buses roll past, showing the city losing money. White city leaders sit together and refuse to listen to the protestors.

pages.text: The protestors didn’t give up. The boycott continued for over a year. Finally, in December 1956, segregation on city buses became illegal. The protest was successful. It showed that change was possible. It helped King become a well-known leader of the civil rights movement. The Women of the Bus Protest Black women played an important part in desegregating Montgomery buses. Even before Parks refused to give up her seat in 1955, Black women were working to change how Black people were treated on buses in Montgomery. While five Black women took the fight to court, others kept the bus boycott going. They organized meetings, arranged carpools, and talked to protestors. Their efforts helped the boycott continue until the protestors’ demands were met. Martin Luther King Jr.
pages.brief: The Montgomery bus boycott continues for over a year. Black women organize meetings, arrange carpools, and talk with protestors. Five Black women take the fight to court. In December 1956, segregation on city buses becomes illegal. Martin Luther King Jr. is now known as a civil rights leader.

pages.text: The Birmingham Protests Segregation and violence against Black people continued in the South. White people who wanted segregation bombed the houses of Black leaders, including King’s. This didn’t stop King. In 1957, he and other Black leaders formed a civil rights organization. As president of the organization, King traveled and spoke about civil rights. In April 1963, King went to Birmingham, Alabama, to help organize a protest against segregation. Hundreds of people were arrested during the peaceful protest, including King. Black leaders raised money to get the protestors out of jail. During another march the next month, protestors were stopped by police. The police used fire hoses and attack dogs. Many of the protestors were badly hurt. Hundreds were arrested.
pages.brief: In Birmingham, Alabama, Martin Luther King Jr. helps organize a peaceful protest against segregation. Police arrest hundreds, including King. Black leaders raise money to free protestors. During another march, police stop protestors with fire hoses and attack dogs, hurting many. A bombed house shows the violence against Black leaders.

pages.text: When people across the country heard about what happened to the protestors, they were angry. Black leaders and city leaders made a deal a week later. Birmingham had to desegregate. People Who Inspired King Dr. Benjamin Mays (1894–1984) Mays was a minister and the president of the school King attended. He became a teacher to King. Howard Thurman (1899–1981) Thurman was a minister and King’s teacher at school. He taught King about peaceful protests. Mohandas Gandhi (1869–1948) Gandhi was a leader in India. His ideas about peaceful protest inspired King. Bayard Rustin (1912–1987) Rustin was a leader and King’s friend. He helped organize a famous march in Washington, D.C., in 1963. Martin Luther King Jr.
pages.brief: People across the country react angrily to the violence in Birmingham. A week later, Black leaders and city leaders make a deal: Birmingham must desegregate. Four portraits show people who inspired King: Benjamin Mays, Howard Thurman, Mohandas Gandhi, and Bayard Rustin, each in a setting tied to teaching, peace, or organizing.

pages.text: The Work Continues A few months after the Birmingham protests, King and other Black leaders organized the March on Washington. The march was to protest how Black people were treated in the United States. Thousands of people joined the march. King gave a famous speech. He called for justice and equality for all people. The next year, in 1964, the president of the United States signed the Civil Rights Act. It made segregation of public places against the law.
pages.brief: Martin Luther King Jr. stands before thousands of people at the March on Washington. He gives a famous speech calling for justice and equality for all people. A few months later, in 1964, the president of the United States signs the Civil Rights Act, making segregation of public places against the law.

pages.text: Many white people still wanted segregation, though, and the fight for civil rights continued. In 1965, violence broke out during a peaceful protest in Selma, Alabama. Leaders were working to sign up Black voters there. Although Black people had the right to vote, white officials often kept them from doing so. On March 7, 1965, King helped plan a march from Selma to Montgomery to protest how Black voters were treated. King led the marchers, but they didn’t get far before police attacked them. Three weeks later, the protestors marched again. This time, members of the U.S. Army sent by the president protected the protestors. Martin Luther King Jr.
pages.brief: In Selma, Alabama, Martin Luther King Jr. helps plan a march from Selma to Montgomery to protest how Black voters are treated. King leads the marchers until police attack them. Three weeks later, protestors march again, this time protected by members of the U.S. Army sent by the president.

pages.text: On August 6, 1965, the president signed the Voting Rights Act into law. It protected the right of all people of color to vote. The Right to Vote Although all Black people had the right to vote by 1920, state and local laws kept them from doing so. Election officials forced Black voters to take unfair tests or pay money before they could vote. Sometimes white people in the community threatened and attacked Black people if they tried to vote. Congress passed the Voting Rights Act to address these problems. The Act helped. However, there was a change to the law in 2013. The change allowed state leaders to pass new voting laws. They say the laws keep voting fair. Others say some of these laws make it harder for Black people and other people of color to vote.
pages.brief: The president signs the Voting Rights Act on August 6, 1965. In a voting scene, election officials give Black voters unfair tests and demand money before they can vote. Other Black people face threats. Later, state leaders pass new voting laws, while supporters and opponents disagree about whether those laws keep voting fair.

pages.text: King’s Memorial In 1968, King traveled to Tennessee to support a workers’ protest. While there, a white man shot and killed him. King died on April 4. People around the world were shocked and sad about his death. In 2011, a memorial opened in Washington, D.C., to honor King. People from all over the world visit the memorial. They remember this great man as the work toward justice and equality for all people continues. Martin Luther King Jr.
pages.brief: In 1968, Martin Luther King Jr. travels to Tennessee to support a workers’ protest. A white man shoots and kills him there on April 4. People around the world are shocked and sad. In 2011, a memorial opens in Washington, D.C., where visitors honor King as the work for justice and equality continues.

books.title: The Story of the Statue
books.art_why: The keyword check calls for drawing, and the book covers historical events from the 1800s.

pages.text: Introduction The Statue of Liberty is a famous monument in the United States. It is a great work of art that is important to our country’s past, present, and future.
pages.brief: The Statue of Liberty is shown as a famous monument in the United States, standing as a great work of art that is important to the country’s past, present, and future; a wide view presents it as a national monument.

pages.text: Super-Sized Statue The Statue of Liberty looks like a giant green woman! It weighs about 450,000 pounds, or as much as 115 cars. From the ground to the tip of its torch, it is 305 ½ feet—as tall as a 30-story building. From head to toe, it is 111 ½ feet tall—taller than three school buses stacked end to end.
pages.brief: The Statue of Liberty appears as a giant green woman, shown from the ground to the tip of its torch beside a 30-story building, 115 cars, and three school buses stacked end to end to show its huge size.

pages.text: The statue is located on an island near New York. As the tallest statue in the United States, Lady Liberty can be seen from miles away. Where did this famous monument come from?
pages.brief: The Statue of Liberty stands on an island near New York, the tallest statue in the United States, and it can be seen from miles away across the water as people wonder where this famous monument came from.

pages.text: An Idea Is Born Edouard de Laboulaye, a French historian, admired the United States. In 1865, he gave a dinner party. One of the guests was the sculptor Auguste Bartholdi. Mr. Laboulaye told Mr. Bartholdi that he wanted to give a gift of friendship to the United States. The gift was the Statue of Liberty.
pages.brief: At a dinner party in 1865, French historian Edouard de Laboulaye speaks with sculptor Auguste Bartholdi about a gift of friendship to the United States, the Statue of Liberty; the two men are seated together at the table.

pages.text: Mr. Bartholdi began planning the statue in 1871. First, he suggested that they build it on Bedloe’s Island, in New York Harbor. The Americans thought about it and agreed. Then, Mr. Bartholdi made a clay model of the statue. The model was finished in 1875. The statue needed to last through wind and bad weather. So the French engineer Gustave Eiffel agreed to help. He created a strong iron skeleton for the statue. He also had the idea to cover the outside with 300 sheets of thin copper.
pages.brief: Auguste Bartholdi plans the statue in 1871, with Bedloe’s Island in New York Harbor behind him; he works on a clay model while Gustave Eiffel designs a strong iron skeleton and thin copper sheets for the statue.

pages.text: Made in France, Moved to America The statue was expensive. France agreed to build and pay for the statue. The United States agreed to build and pay for its pedestal. Both countries asked people to donate money for the cause. Even children gave their spare coins and dollars. In 1876, the United States borrowed the statue’s arm and torch. It was put on display to help raise money. People saw part of the statue and wanted to give even more money.
pages.brief: In France and the United States, people donate money for the statue and its pedestal, including children giving spare coins; in 1876 the statue’s arm and torch are displayed in America to raise more funds.

pages.text: In 1878, the statue’s head was finished and displayed in Paris. The statue’s arm and torch were returned to France in 1882. Finally, in 1884, the entire statue was put together. Then the French took the statue apart! The pieces were packed into 214 crates and put on a ship to the United States. The ship arrived in 1885.
pages.brief: In Paris in 1878 the statue’s finished head is displayed; later the whole statue is put together in 1884, taken apart, packed into 214 crates, and loaded on a ship that arrives in the United States in 1885.

pages.text: The Statue of Liberty was placed on its pedestal in 1886—ten years late! It was supposed to be given to the United States in 1876. This date was 100 years after the United States declared its independence. People were still happy, though. They held a celebration with music and a parade. President Grover Cleveland even gave a speech.
pages.brief: In 1886 the Statue of Liberty is placed on its pedestal, ten years later than planned; the people are still happy, and crowds celebrate with music and a parade as President Grover Cleveland gives a speech.

pages.text: Symbolism of the Statue The statue is more than a work of art. It is a symbol of friendship between two countries. It also stands for the freedom and hope of people who have moved to the United States. A poem on display inside the pedestal includes the famous lines, “Give me your tired, your poor, Your huddled masses yearning to breathe free.”
pages.brief: The Statue of Liberty stands as a symbol of friendship between two countries and of freedom and hope for people who moved to the United States; inside the pedestal, a poem with famous lines is on display.

pages.text: Certain parts of the statue have special meaning as well. The crown has seven spikes, which stand for the seven seas and continents of the world. The torch in the statue’s right hand is a symbol of freedom. The tablet in the statue’s left hand has the date July 4, 1776, written on it. This is the date when the Declaration of Independence was signed.
pages.brief: Close views show the Statue of Liberty’s crown with seven spikes, its right-hand torch, and its left-hand tablet marked with July 4, 1776; each part has special meaning and stands for freedom, the world, and American independence.

pages.text: Liberty for All The Statue of Liberty has stood the test of time, though it has needed some repairs. American workers have made the iron skeleton stronger and have added many lights. The statue started out the color of a shiny, new copper penny. The air slowly made it change color. By the 1920s, it had turned green!
pages.brief: American workers strengthen the Statue of Liberty’s iron skeleton and add many lights; the statue changes from the color of a shiny new copper penny to green as the air slowly affects it by the 1920s.

pages.text: Millions of people from all over the world visit the Statue of Liberty each year. They take a ferry to the island, which is now called Liberty Island. They were once able to climb to the torch. Today, however, visitors are only allowed inside the pedestal and crown. People will continue to visit the statue for many years to see this symbol of freedom.
pages.brief: Millions of visitors from around the world ride a ferry to Liberty Island and see the Statue of Liberty; today they may go inside the pedestal and crown, and people will keep visiting this symbol of freedom for many years.

books.title: Remembering September 11
books.art_why: Photographs exist of the 2001 attacks, the memorials built afterwards, and the yearly ceremonies.

pages.text: On September 11, 2001, a group of terrorists hijacked four planes on the East Coast of the United States. They crashed the first two planes on purpose into the World Trade Center towers in New York City. Soon after, they smashed a third plane into the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia. They tried to crash a fourth plane into another building, but people on the plane stopped them. That plane crashed in a field in Pennsylvania. The tragic events of that day left many people dead or injured. The Twin Towers were completely destroyed, and their collapse caused damage many blocks away. An entire section of the Pentagon was destroyed as well.
pages.brief: Four hijacked planes on the East Coast: two crash into the World Trade Center towers in New York City, one into the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia, and one into a field in Pennsylvania. The Twin Towers collapse, wreckage is scattered for blocks, and a section of the Pentagon is destroyed.

pages.text: Many people became heroes because of their brave actions that day. Police, firefighters, doctors, nurses, and ordinary people who were just walking by ran into burning buildings to help people who were trapped or hurt. Rescue workers from all over the United States came to help find survivors. Some of these heroes died trying to help.
pages.brief: Police officers, firefighters, doctors and nurses run into burning buildings to reach people trapped or hurt, joined by ordinary people who were walking by. Rescue workers from all over the United States arrive to search for survivors, and some of these heroes die while helping.

pages.text: Beginning to Remember In the days after September 11, people wanted to show their support for the survivors and heroes, and to remember the people who died. They wanted to make sure the events and people were never forgotten. The sites around the plane crashes were covered with cards, pictures, letters, American flags, and other special objects. People also covered the walls and sidewalks outside police and fire stations with remembrances.
pages.brief: At the crash sites, cards, pictures, letters, American flags and other special objects pile up. Outside police and fire stations, people cover the walls and sidewalks with remembrances, showing support for survivors and heroes and remembering those who died.

pages.text: In New York City, people lit thousands of candles in different parks and wrote messages of support on long rolls of paper. Volunteers gave their time to help the rescue workers as they searched for survivors and cleaned up the debris. They gathered food and other supplies that the rescue workers needed.
pages.brief: In New York City parks, thousands of candles are lit and long rolls of paper carry messages of support. Volunteers give their time to help rescue workers search for survivors and clean up debris, gathering the food and supplies the workers need.

pages.text: The Spreading Memorials People all over the world began to send cards, letters, and other things to show their support. A group of children in Hawaii made leis— necklaces made of flowers—with messages written on them. They sent these messages to survivors and rescue workers at all three sites. The leis gave people hope and support. Many children used art to show the world how they felt about September 11. Some drew, painted, and colored pictures of what they saw that day to help them process the events. Others sent letters of support with their art to the rescue workers, survivors, and families of those who died.
pages.brief: Children in Hawaii make flower leis with messages written on them and send them to survivors and rescue workers at all three sites. Other children draw, paint and color pictures of what they saw, sending their art and letters of support to workers, survivors and families.

pages.text: Permanent Memorials As time passed, people wanted more permanent ways to remember September 11. Towns all across the United States found their own ways to do this. Some put up statues or sculptures, and others dedicated beautiful gardens.
pages.brief: In towns across the United States, people look for lasting ways to remember September 11. Some towns put up statues or sculptures, while others dedicate beautiful gardens as permanent memorials where people can come and remember.

pages.text: Bayonne, New Jersey, which overlooks where the Twin Towers once stood, put up a large sculpture. The memorial, which was donated by a Russian artist, looks like a tower with an open crack in the middle. A metal teardrop hanging down in the center stands for the sadness people felt after September 11. Do You Know? The U.S. Mint, the government body that makes coins and medals, made two million of these medals to help remember September 11 and raise money for the memorial in New York City.
pages.brief: In Bayonne, New Jersey, overlooking where the Twin Towers once stood, a large sculpture donated by a Russian artist rises. It looks like a tower with an open crack in the middle, and a metal teardrop hangs down in the center, standing for the sadness people felt.

pages.text: Memorials at the Sites New York City wanted to put up a memorial at the site where the World Trade Center towers were destroyed. In 2003, the city held a competition to find a design. Over five thousand people from sixty-three nations sent in their designs. From those thousands, only eight designs were chosen as finalists. The city chose a design in 2004. It took nearly seven years to build the memorial before it opened on September 11, 2011.
pages.brief: In 2003 New York City holds a competition for a memorial design, and more than five thousand people from sixty-three nations send in designs. Eight become finalists, and the city chooses one in 2004. Building takes nearly seven years before the memorial opens.

pages.text: The memorial in New York City has two huge pools of water where the Twin Towers once stood. The country’s largest artificial waterfalls flow into the pools, around which 2,983 names are carved. These are the names of the victims of all three September 11 attacks and another attack on the Twin Towers on February 26, 1993.
pages.brief: Two huge pools of water sit where the Twin Towers once stood, with the country's largest artificial waterfalls flowing into them. Around the pools, the names of 2,983 victims of all three September 11 attacks and the 1993 bombing are carved.

pages.text: In Pennsylvania, the National Park Service held a competition to find a design for its own memorial. Over one thousand people sent in their designs, but only one was chosen. The wall is made of forty pieces of marble. Each piece of marble has the name of one passenger who died in the plane crash carved into it. The memorial wall follows the plane’s flight path to a large boulder in a field. The boulder marks the crash site.
pages.brief: In Pennsylvania, a memorial wall of forty pieces of marble follows the plane's flight path across a field to a large boulder that marks the crash site. Each piece of marble carries the carved name of one passenger who died in the crash.

pages.text: The Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia, opened a memorial on September 11, 2008. It has 184 benches. The name of a victim who died at the Pentagon is carved into the end of each one. To read the names, a person must face the south side of the building, where the plane crashed. At night, bright lights shine from underneath the benches.
pages.brief: The Pentagon memorial in Arlington, Virginia, has 184 benches, each with a victim's name carved into its end. A person reading a name faces the south side of the building, where the plane crashed. At night, bright lights shine from underneath the benches.

pages.text: Ceremonies Every year on September 11, the people in charge of these memorials and others around the United States hold special ceremonies. People from the United States and other countries around the world come to watch and participate in them.
pages.brief: Every year on September 11, the people in charge of these memorials and of others around the United States hold special ceremonies. People from the United States and from other countries around the world come to watch and to take part.
