pages.brief: A group of plants stands together in a garden. Most have four common parts: roots in soil, stems, green leaves, and flowers. A few nearby plants look clearly different, hinting at the unusual plants explored next.

pages.text: Plants commonly called air plants live in trees high above the ground near ponds, streams, rivers, and swamps in North and South America. These plants don’t live in soil as most plants do—they live on tree branches! Instead of getting water from the soil through their roots, they get moisture from the air through their leaves. They only use their roots to hold tight to branches.
pages.brief: Air plants cling to tree branches high above a pond or stream in a warm, humid American landscape. Their leaves absorb moisture from the air, while their roots hold tightly to the bark instead of growing in soil.

pages.text: Unbelievable though it may seem, plants exist that eat meat. They eat insects, spiders, and even some fish, amphibians, reptiles, and small mammals. Like all plants, they use sunlight and water to produce their own food. However, the soil they grow in doesn’t provide them with everything they need to be healthy. The animals they “eat” on the side help them grow better.
pages.brief: A carnivorous plant grows in poor soil, with an insect trapped in its leaves. Sunlight and water help it make food. Around it are tiny clues of other prey, showing that some plants eat insects, spiders, and even small animals.

pages.text: One well-known meat-eating, or carnivorous, plant is the Venus flytrap. This plant lives in moist environments. Its leaves look like traps with small spikes along the edges and special hairs on the inside. When a critter walks inside a leaf and brushes against the hairs, the leaf snaps shut. The critter is trapped by the spikes.
pages.brief: A Venus flytrap grows in a moist environment. Its open leaf looks like a trap with small spikes along the edges and special hairs inside. A small critter walks in and brushes the hairs, and the leaf snaps shut.

pages.text: The sundew, another carnivorous plant that lives in moist environments, catches its food in a different way. Sticky hairs on its surface smell sweet. Insects attracted to the smell land and get stuck. Then the plant digests the insects. The giant sundew plant of Australia even eats small frogs!
pages.brief: A sundew plant grows in a moist environment, its surface covered with sticky hairs that smell sweet. An insect lands and becomes stuck. Nearby, a giant sundew shows how the plant can even catch small frogs.

pages.text: Some plants steal food from other plants. The dodder plant lives on many continents but is most common in North and South America. It sends slender rootlike stems into another plant and sucks food and water from the plant. The dodder plant is a parasite —a living thing that lives off another living thing. When a dodder plant attaches to a plant to feed, its connection to the soil dies.
pages.brief: A dodder plant, common in the Americas, sends slender, rootlike stems into another plant and sucks food and water from it. The dodder is a parasite. Where it attaches to feed, its own connection to the soil dies away.

pages.text: Many flowers have bad smells that attract insects. The stapelia flower, also called the “carrion flower,” smells like rotting meat. On hot days, the odor is noticeable from about 1.6 kilometers (1 mi.) away. The flower has a pattern that looks like dead animals. Flies are attracted to the pattern as well as the smell, so they fly into the flower. Special powder called “pollen” gets on their bodies, and they carry it to other flowers. The flowers use the powder to make seeds and grow new plants.
pages.brief: A stapelia flower opens in hot sun, its patterned surface looking like dead animals. The rotting-meat odor travels far. A fly lands, drawn by the smell, and pollen sticks to its body to be carried to another flower.

pages.text: Some plants look like stones. The plants in this photograph are called “stone plants” or “living stones.” They live in very hot, dry places such as South Africa. They hold water very well because the biggest part of each plant lives underground. These plants are tiny and usually have only two leaves. Their shape helps them hide so animals don’t eat them.
pages.brief: Tiny stone plants sit among rocks in a hot, dry South African place. Most of each plant hides underground, holding water. Only two leaves show above the ground, shaped to blend in so animals do not eat them.

pages.text: Some cactus plants are covered with wool- like hairs. These plants come from Bolivia and Peru, high in the Andes Mountains of South America. The “wool” protects them from daytime heat and nighttime cold. It also helps the cactus plants hold moisture.
pages.brief: A woolly cactus stands high in the Andes Mountains of Bolivia or Peru. Soft, wool-like hairs cover its body, protecting it from daytime heat and nighttime cold while helping it hold moisture in the dry mountain air.

pages.text: Some trees and shrubs grow out of solid rock. They grow up high where the wind blows strong. The wind can blow seeds into small cracks in the rock. When rain gets into the cracks, the seeds start to grow. Their roots reach down into small cracks for moisture. As the roots continue to grow, they split the rock.
pages.brief: A tree grows out of solid rock high where strong wind blows. A seed landed in a small crack, rain helped it sprout, and its roots reach down for moisture. As the roots grow, they split the rock apart.

pages.text: Some plants have animals living inside them. Ant colonies live inside ant plants. The ants protect the plant from animals that would eat it. They use spaces in the plant’s stem as houses. Some spaces are used for raising young ants, while other spaces are used for garbage. The ant plant uses some of this garbage for food.
pages.brief: An ant plant holds an ant colony inside its stem. Ants move through spaces used as houses for raising young and for garbage. The ants protect the plant from animals that would eat it, and the plant uses some garbage for food.

pages.text: Many more kinds of strange plants also exist. Bamboo makes noise when it grows, and some Australian orchids grow and flower completely underground. Bat plants have fruit that looks like bats hanging upside down from the flowers. Some ghost plants have white flowers that seem to appear out of nowhere. There are many amazing plants in the world.
pages.brief: A gathering of strange plants: bamboo grows noisily, an Australian orchid flowers completely underground, a bat plant hangs fruit shaped like bats, and ghost plants show white flowers that seem to appear from nowhere. Each one is unusual.

books.title: Sugar, Sugar, Everywhere
books.art_why: Sugar, foods, factories, drinks, and health topics all exist in the real world today, so photographs fit best.

pages.text: Introduction Which ingredient makes desserts and treats taste sweet? It’s sugar! You might be surprised to learn that desserts and treats are not the only foods that have sugar in them. In fact, people add sugar to many foods you wouldn’t expect.
pages.brief: A tabletop spread of sweet desserts and treats, such as a slice of cake, cookies, and candy, beside a few ordinary everyday foods, showing that sugar is not only in desserts; the foods sit on a clean kitchen table in soft natural light.

pages.text: What Is Sugar? Sugar is a natural part of plant foods and milk. Apples, pears, and grapes are full of natural sugar. Many vegetables contain sugar and starch, which breaks down into sugar. The white crystals in a sugar bowl are table sugar, which is different from the sugar found in fruits and vegetables.
pages.brief: A close-up photo of apples, pears, and grapes grouped with fresh vegetables and a glass of milk; nearby sits a small bowl of white sugar crystals. The natural foods and the sugar bowl are on a wooden kitchen table in bright daylight.

pages.text: When we eat sugar and starch, our body changes them into a simple sugar called glucose. Glucose is carried by the blood to all parts of the body, and provides the energy that keeps our body parts working. The body needs this glucose to stay alive.
pages.brief: A close-up photo of a hand holding a ripe apple and a piece of bread above a plate, with a faint red-tinted view of blood vessels in the background to suggest glucose traveling through the body and providing energy; the setting is a simple kitchen table.

pages.text: What Happens to Sugar We Eat?
pages.brief: A simple, quiet image with no people or objects: soft, pale swirls of light on an empty background, suggesting a question about sugar. The page keeps the focus only on wondering what happens to sugar we eat.

pages.text: Where Sugar Is Found The body can get all the sugar it needs from naturally sweet and starchy foods. Many processed foods, which are made by machines in factories, are packed with extra sugar. Cakes, cookies, ice cream, and candy are all processed with added sugar in them.
pages.brief: A bright food factory interior where machines move cakes, cookies, ice cream containers, and candy along a production line; the processed sweets are being packed with added sugar in a clean industrial setting.

pages.text: Sugar is also added to foods you might not expect, such as processed tomato sauce and ketchup. Many low-fat sauces and salad dressings contain sugar, too, since sugar is often used to replace fat in those foods.
pages.brief: On a kitchen counter, a bottle of ketchup and a jar of processed tomato sauce sit beside low-fat salad dressing and sauce bottles; a small dish of sugar is nearby, showing added sugar in foods people might not expect.

pages.text: Breakfast cereal can be another source of added sugar because many cereals have colorful sugary treats added to them. Even cereals with plain flakes may have a dusting of sugar to make them taste sweeter. How much sugar is in these breakfast cereals? 1 cup Grams of sugar Shredded Wheat (no frosting) 0g Toasted Oats 1g Corn Flakes 2g Crisp Rice 3g Raisin Bran 18g.
pages.brief: Several bowls of breakfast cereal on a table: plain shredded wheat, toasted oats, corn flakes, crisp rice, and raisin bran. Some cereals have colorful sugary pieces; others look like plain flakes with a light dusting of sugar. A cup measure sits beside them.

pages.text: Sugar and Health Remember, people need glucose to stay alive. When someone has too little glucose in their blood, their body does not have the energy it needs. But too much glucose in the blood can also be bad because it can damage the body.
pages.brief: A photo of a person sitting tired with low energy beside a plate of food, while a second image shows a body outline with too much glucose; the scene suggests both too little and too much glucose can affect the body.

pages.text: Over a long time, high glucose levels can strain some parts of the body, such as the heart, brain, and eyes, making it hard for them to work as they should. Do You Know? For some people, sweetened drinks are the biggest source of added sugar. Soda pop and fruit-flavored drinks make up almost half of the added sugar in some people’s diets.
pages.brief: A close-up of a glass of soda and a fruit-flavored drink on a table, with a faint image of a heart, brain, and eyes in the background to suggest strain from high glucose; the drinks are the focus in a bright kitchen.

pages.text: Making Healthy Choices How can people avoid eating too much added sugar? One way is to eat more natural foods such as fresh fruits and vegetables, which have no added sugar. Another way is to eat homemade meals. Food that is cooked at home is often healthier than processed foods.
pages.brief: A family-style kitchen scene with fresh fruits and vegetables on a counter and a homemade meal being prepared; no packaged processed foods are in view, showing a way to avoid added sugar by eating natural foods and home-cooked meals.

pages.text: People can also limit added sugar by choosing healthier options when snacking. For example, plain yogurt sweetened with fresh fruit and nuts is a better option than donuts or cookies.
pages.brief: On a kitchen table, a bowl of plain yogurt topped with fresh fruit and nuts sits beside a plate of donuts and cookies; the yogurt snack is in the foreground, showing a healthier choice for limiting added sugar.

pages.text: Sugar makes food taste sweeter, but eating too much added sugar can harm our health. Natural sugar and starch provide plenty of energy to fuel our bodies and keep us going. Fresh fruits and vegetables not only taste good, they are also good for the body!
pages.brief: A bright table display of fresh fruits and vegetables beside a small bowl of sugar; the natural foods look colorful and appetizing, while the sugar bowl is smaller, showing that natural sugar and starch fuel the body and fresh produce is good for health.

books.title: Electric Eels!
books.art_why: The book includes an 1800 expedition and historical scenes, so drawings fit.

pages.text: Legendary Shocker Alexander Humboldt went to South America to catch electric eels in 1800. He thought they could help him learn about electricity, a kind of energy that scientists knew little about. He knew not to touch the eels because their shocks could cause great pain. He asked some fishermen to help.
pages.brief: In South America in 1800, Alexander Humboldt stands near a river with fishermen. He looks at electric eels in the water but keeps his hands back, knowing their shocks cause great pain. He asks the fishermen to help him catch the eels.

pages.text: The fishermen led about thirty horses into a pond. The electric eels began to shock the horses. When the eels were too tired to shock the horses anymore, the fishermen caught five eels. Humboldt learned much about the eels. Shocking Fish Story Recently, a scientist saw eels rise up to protect themselves as they did with the horses. Before that, some scientists thought Humboldt might not have been telling the truth.
pages.brief: In a shallow South American pond, fishermen lead about thirty horses into the water. Long electric eels rise and shock the horses. When the eels are too tired to shock, the fishermen catch five eels while Alexander Humboldt learns much about the eels.

pages.text: It’s a Fish! Electric eels are long gray-brown fish with yellow or orange on their throats. They are more like catfish than other eels and belong to a group of fish that are all electric. Electric eels can be about as big around as an adult person’s leg and three times as long. Male and female electric eels are alike in color and size. Electric Eel Facts Scientific Name Electrophorus electricus Animal Type Fish Diet Fish, crustaceans, and amphibians Length 2 to 3 meters (7–10 feet) Weight 20 to 22 kilograms (44–48 pounds)
pages.brief: A long gray-brown electric eel with a yellow-orange throat swims in dark water. Its thick body is compared with an adult person’s leg, and its length is three times as long. A male and a female eel, alike in color and size, are shown nearby.

pages.text: Unlike most other fish, electric eels breathe air. They have gills, but their gills mostly help them breathe out. Electric eels have special organs in their mouths that help them breathe in. They breathe out waste air from their mouths and gills. They come up to breathe air every few minutes and can drown if they don’t.
pages.brief: An electric eel rises to the water’s surface to breathe air. Its mouth is open as it takes in air, while waste air leaves through its mouth and gills. The eel has gills but mostly uses them to breathe out; it must come up every few minutes or drown.

pages.text: Like most other fish, electric eels have fins and a backbone. Their backbones and fins are body parts that help them move. They swim slowly most of the time, but they move quickly when they attack. Shocking Fact Electric eels can grow new tails if theirs are cut off.
pages.brief: An electric eel swims slowly through river water, its fins and backbone helping it move along its long body. Then it darts quickly to attack. Beside it, a tail is shown regrowing after being cut off.

pages.text: It’s Electric! Electric eels are the most electric fish on Earth. They can find their way around and send signals to other eels using their electricity. They can also protect themselves, hunt, and stun or kill the animals they eat. Other fish use electricity, too, but none are as powerful as electric eels. Shocking Medical History Don’t try this at home! Ancient Greeks and Romans tried to cure headaches with electric rays. A ray’s shock could have made a person’s head numb, so it might have worked! Other Electric Fish.
pages.brief: An electric eel sends electricity through river water to find its way and signal other eels. It also uses shocks to hunt and protect itself. In a separate scene, an ancient Greek or Roman person holds an electric ray near their head, hoping the shock will cure a headache.

pages.text: Three organs make an electric eel’s shocks. These organs make up most of an electric eel’s body. They make its body like a big battery that could turn on a light. Shocking Fact If an electric eel curls its head to its tail, its shocking power becomes greater. Three Electric Organs.
pages.brief: Inside a long electric eel, three electric organs fill most of its body. The organs are shown working together like a big battery that could turn on a light. The eel curls its head toward its tail, making its shocking power greater.

pages.text: An electric eel can shock its prey, or the animals it eats, with up to 650 volts of electricity. The shock can kill small animals and stun big ones. Any animal near the eel can feel it. The shock has about five times the volts used to power a lamp. Scientists don’t know why electric eels can’t feel their own shocks. It might be because of how big the eels are. It might be because of how their shock moves. Or it might be because electric eels have body parts that protect them. Electric eels have long rows of special cells called electrocytes. Electrocytes each send out a tiny shock at almost the same time. The cells work together to create the electric eel’s big attack ZAP!
pages.brief: An electric eel releases a powerful shock in river water that can kill small animals and stun big ones. Rows of special cells along its body send tiny shocks almost together to create the big zap. The shock is compared with the power of a lamp, and the eel is shown unharmed by its own electricity.

pages.text: Stunning Attack Before an electric eel uses its attack zap, it has to find prey. Electric eels can’t see well and are nocturnal, or most active at night. Electric eels send out small shocks—about fifty every second—to sense nearby plants and animals. When an electric eel senses prey, it sends out two or three big shocks. The shocks make the prey move, which helps the eel find it quickly. Then the electric eel sends out its attack shock, which stuns or kills the prey. The electric eel sucks the prey into its belly before the animal swims away. Electric eels mostly eat small fish or animals like frogs or shrimp. Young eels also eat worms and insects.
pages.brief: At night in a South American river, an electric eel sends small shocks through the water to sense plants and animals. When it senses prey, it sends two or three bigger shocks, then an attack shock that stuns or kills. The eel sucks the prey into its belly.

pages.text: Don’t Swim There! Electric eels are top predators that few other animals eat in the South American rivers where they live. They can also live in other types of nearby fresh water, such as ponds. Because they breathe air, electric eels can live in water that might kill other fish. They can also live out of water for hours if they stay wet. Electric Eel Habitat ATLANTIC OCEAN SOUTH AMERICA PACIFIC OCEAN.
pages.brief: On a map of South America between the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans, electric eels are shown in rivers and ponds. They are top predators that few animals eat. Because they breathe air, they can live in water that would kill other fish and stay out of water for hours if wet.

pages.text: Electric eels mostly lay eggs in small ponds. Male eels build bubble nests with their spit. Female eels lay eggs in the bubbles. Males protect the nest. They also protect the babies until they grow to about half as long as a pencil. The young eels only make small shocks, so they can become prey for other animals.
pages.brief: In a small pond, a male electric eel builds a nest of bubbles with its spit. A female lays eggs in the bubbles. The male guards the nest and the babies until they are about half as long as a pencil. Young eels make only small shocks.

pages.text: Future Energy Source Scientists are still learning new things about electric eels. Some scientists want to use what they have learned about electric eels to make a new kind of battery. The battery could be used inside people, and it wouldn’t harm them or run out of power. Two hundred years ago, Humboldt wrote that scientists didn’t understand all the secrets of electric fish. That is still true today. What will electric eels help scientists learn next?
pages.brief: Scientists study an electric eel and a new kind of battery. They hope to use what they learn to make a battery that could go inside people without harming them or running out of power. A portrait of Alexander Humboldt recalls his words from two hundred years ago.

books.title: King George III
books.art_why: A biography of a named famous person, King George III, so it is drawn rather than photographed.

pages.brief: A plain, quiet opening page with a soft paper texture and a thin decorative border, showing no people, places or objects, just empty space where the book's picture credits are listed.

pages.text: King King George III George III King King George III George III King King George III George III.
pages.brief: A simple, formal title page with an ornamental border and clean empty space, showing nothing except the decoration around the edges of the page.

pages.text: Meeting George III John Adams, one of America’s first leaders, traveled to England and stood before King George III. The year was 1785, and Adams had the difficult task of making peace between the two countries. America had recently won its freedom in a war against Great Britain. Adams spoke with the king, offering America’s friendship. He spoke highly of the king and wished him good health and happiness. The king smiled. George III may have lost the American colonies, but he knew he would make Great Britain strong again.
pages.brief: In England in 1785, John Adams stands before King George III in a grand room, offering America's friendship and wishing the king good health. The king, seated and wearing royal dress, smiles back at him.

pages.text: Early Life King George III was born on June 4, 1738. His father and mother were the Prince and Princess of Wales. His grandfather, King George II, was the king of England. Young George grew up in an unhappy family. His father, Frederick, was first in line to be king. Frederick argued with his father, the king. George disliked hearing his father and grandfather fight. Then, at just twelve years old, George’s father died, making George first in line to the British throne. Someday, he would be king.
pages.brief: Young George grows up in an unhappy royal household, shown as a boy watching his father Frederick argue with his grandfather, King George II. Then, at twelve, George stands sorrowfully as his father dies, leaving him first in line for the throne.

pages.text: To prepare to be king, George studied harder. Lord Bute, a nobleman, taught George about how British government worked. As king, George would have a ministry, or group of advisors. Another group, called Parliament, made laws for the nation. The king and Parliament often disagreed. George would need to know how to solve problems. In 1760, George’s grandfather died, and George became king of Great Britain and Ireland at the age of twenty-two. At the time, Britain was fighting France and other countries in a European battle called the Seven Years’ War. Soon the war spread to North America.
pages.brief: Lord Bute, a nobleman, teaches young George about British government, pointing to papers as the prince studies. Later, in 1760, the twenty-two-year-old George is crowned king while Britain fights France in the Seven Years' War.

pages.text: A Huge Empire In North America, the war was called the French and Indian War. Great Britain was already powerful, but when they defeated the French in North America and in Europe, they controlled more land than ever before. The war caused fighting between Lord Bute and William Pitt, one of the king’s ministers. Pitt wanted to keep fighting, but Bute didn’t. The king sided with Lord Bute and gave him the top job in his ministry. From there, Bute brought an end to the war in 1763 and quit his position shortly after that. North American British Territories in 1763.
pages.brief: British soldiers defeat French soldiers in North America and Europe, taking more land than ever before. In Britain, Lord Bute and William Pitt argue over the war, and the king sides with Bute, who ends the fighting in 1763.

pages.text: A Royal Family of His Own Not long after becoming king, George married German princess Sophia Charlotte in 1761. Their marriage lasted for more than fifty years, and they had fifteen children. Happy at home, the king continued to learn all he could and studied more about history and government. He learned the names of all the ships in the Royal Navy. He took his job as king seriously, and he faced big problems. Simple Tastes Even though he was from a royal family, King George enjoyed simpler things. He loved agriculture and spent many days inspecting his kingdom’s farms. His favorite activities included horseback riding, music, attending the theater, and playing cards.
pages.brief: King George marries German princess Sophia Charlotte in 1761, and the couple sit surrounded by their fifteen children in a warm family home. Elsewhere the king rides horses, inspects farms, enjoys music, attends the theater and plays cards.

pages.text: Trouble in America The British colonies in America challenged the king more than any others. A huge problem there was about to begin. Great Britain needed money to pay bills from the Seven Years’ War. To get money, England taxed items bought by the colonists. Colonists now had to pay taxes on molasses, printed paper, paint, glass, and tea. They became angry and refused to buy British goods. To protest the taxes, they planned the Boston Tea Party. One night in 1773, a group of colonists climbed aboard a British ship carrying tea in Boston Harbor. The colonists dumped the tea into the water below.
pages.brief: Angry American colonists refuse to buy British goods because of taxes on molasses, printed paper, paint, glass and tea. One night in 1773, colonists climb aboard a British tea ship in Boston Harbor and dump the tea into the water.

pages.text: The colonists’ actions angered the king. Soon the tensions boiled over into war. For Great Britain to win, King George realized he needed more fighting men. He hired a group of German soldiers to help in the fight. Thirty thousand Germans fought next to British troops against the American colonists. The American Revolution went on for seven years. The Americans won the war in 1781. The king said the defeat was not his fault.
pages.brief: Angered by the colonists' actions, King George hires thirty thousand German soldiers to fight beside British troops. After seven years of the American Revolution, the Americans win in 1781, and the king insists the defeat is not his fault.

pages.text: In the years after the American Revolution, the king started acting strangely. He seemed nervous all the time, said odd things, and was confused. He shouted at others and pushed them. Doctors helped the king using the latest treatments. Over time, the king seemed to get better. He returned to his leadership role.
pages.brief: After the American Revolution, King George behaves strangely, looking nervous and confused, shouting at people and pushing them away. Doctors treat him with the latest methods, and over time he seems to get better and returns to leading the country.

pages.text: More Conflicts King George soon faced more challenges, including another war with France. By 1799, France had a new leader—Napoleon Bonaparte. Napoleon wanted to take over Europe, including Great Britain. King George did not want to lose his country. Great Britain and France fought until 1815, when France lost the war. At the same time, a fight started in Ireland. People there felt that Great Britain passed unfair religious laws. The Irish started a rebellion, but Great Britain defeated them.
pages.brief: King George faces new conflicts as Napoleon Bonaparte, France's new leader by 1799, tries to take over Europe including Great Britain. The countries fight until 1815, when France loses, while British troops also defeat a rebellion in Ireland.

pages.text: Later Years King George III was in his fiftieth year as king in 1809, and the country celebrated. The joy would not last long, however. In 1810, the king’s youngest daughter died, which left George heartbroken. George again became mentally and physically ill. The king was unable to finish his royal duties. Parliament allowed Prince George, his son, to rule Great Britain in 1811. In January 1820, King George III died, and his son became King George IV.
pages.brief: In 1809 the country celebrates the king's fiftieth year on the throne, but in 1810 his youngest daughter dies and he is heartbroken, becoming ill again. His son Prince George rules in his place until the king dies in January 1820.

pages.text: New Opinions During his time in power, King George III lost the war with America and slowly became mentally ill. For a long time, many historians thought he was a bad king. Recently, they have changed their opinions of him. George III won two major wars—the Seven Years’ War and the wars with Napoleon. He served as king for sixty years, and he led his country to greatness. Through it all, he remained a good husband and father, and he always put his country first.
pages.brief: Historians reconsider King George III, showing him as a king who won the Seven Years' War and the wars with Napoleon, ruled sixty years and led Britain to greatness, while remaining a good husband and father who put his country first.

pages.text: The Life of George III 1738: George is born on June 4 1751: Frederick, Prince of Wales and George’s father, dies 1756: Seven Years’ War begins 1760: King George II, George’s grandfather, dies, and George becomes king 1763: Seven Years’ War ends 1775: First shots of the American Revolution 1781: The British surrender to the American colonists at Yorktown 1788: George III shows signs of a serious mental illness; resumes duties a year later, appearing to be cured 1798: Britain stops the Irish Rebellion 1809: The king celebrates fifty years on the throne 1815: The British defeat Napoleon 1820: Thousands attend George III’s funeral.
pages.brief: A sweeping view of a royal life in order: a baby born in 1738, a boy losing his father, a young king crowned, a war beginning, British soldiers surrendering at Yorktown, a king ill and recovering, a golden jubilee, and finally a funeral.

books.title: April Fools' Day
books.art_why: The book mixes ancient history and cultural scenes, so drawings fit better than photographs.

pages.text: April Fools’ Day.
pages.brief: A cheerful spring scene with several children laughing together and looking mischievous outdoors under a bright morning sky, hinting at playful April Fools’ fun; fresh green shoots, budding trees, and mild weather suggest early spring.

pages.text: Pranking Fun It’s early spring. Your chili ends up buried under a pile of salt. You’re the victim of an April Fools’ joke. April Fools’ Day is on or near April 1. It’s the one day of the year to play jokes, or pranks, on people.
pages.brief: A surprised child at a kitchen table lifts a spoon from a bowl of chili and finds it buried under salt; a grinning friend stands nearby, having played the prank, while early spring buds show through the window.

pages.text: A common joke may be replacing the sugar with salt. When people see that it’s a joke, yell “April Fools’!” April Fools’ Day.
pages.brief: In a kitchen, a prankster swaps the sugar in a bowl for salt while another person watches; soon a person at the table tastes the salty result and reacts with surprise as someone shouts the joke.

pages.text: Why April First? No one knows why April Fools’ Day is on April 1. It may once have marked the coming of spring. People were often “fooled” by the changing weather at this time of the year. Another idea is that April Fools’ Day began when we first started using the calendar we use today. The start of the new year moved from the beginning of April to January 1. People who still celebrated New Year’s Day on April 1 were called “April fools.” Gotham Goes Mad One story tells how April Fools’ may have started in the English town of Gotham. King John planned to take villagers’ property. The villagers acted like they suffered from insanity to scare King John away. In those days, insanity was thought to be contagious.
pages.brief: A split scene shows fickle spring weather above villagers; beside it, a calendar shifts the new year from April to January, while in the town of Gotham villagers pretend to be insane to frighten King John away.

pages.text: Many celebrations were held in the past near April 1. The ancient Romans celebrated the longer days of spring. They dressed in costumes and played jokes. In Europe in the twelfth century, people celebrated the Feast of Fools. A fake ruler led followers in a parade. People celebrated in this way until the sixteenth century. April Fools’ Day.
pages.brief: Ancient Romans in spring costumes laugh and play jokes outdoors under garlands; in a later European street, a fake ruler leads a lively Feast of Fools parade with followers in festive dress, continuing the celebration.

pages.text: Around the World Today, people celebrate April Fools’ Day differently around the world. Scottish Scramble In Scotland, April Fools’ can go on for two days. On April 1, people in Scotland send friends on foolish tasks. The second day is for playing more jokes. Tips to Avoid Being the April Fool! • Have you read it carefully? Do you really believe there is a cross between a sheep and a pig called a “shig?” • Do you get the feeling you’re being watched? Be on your guard! • Careful! That present may not be what you think.
pages.brief: In a Scottish town, a smiling prankster sends a friend on a silly errand; the next day, another person looks warily around with a suspicious expression and opens a wrapped present, staying on guard for more jokes.

pages.text: French Foolishness In France, April 1 is called “April Fish.” The fish is a person who is easily fooled. People tape paper fish to each other’s backs. April Fools’ Day.
pages.brief: In a French street during a playful April day, one person secretly tapes a paper fish to a friend’s back while others smile; another easily fooled person walks by with a paper fish already stuck behind them.

pages.text: American Tricksters In the United States, the fun lasts all day. Tell a friend that class is canceled or punch holes in his or her water bottle! Other jokes may be to put oil on a doorknob and food color in milk. You may find plastic bugs in food or on your bed. Brazil’s Day of the Lie In Brazil, April 1 is Dia da mentira (Lie Day). People enjoy playing practical jokes, or brincadeiras (breen-kah- DAY-rahs), on each other and tell silly lies all day.
pages.brief: In an American home and classroom, a child tells a friend that class is canceled, another punches holes in a water bottle, and plastic bugs sit near food and on a bed; nearby, Brazilian friends laugh over silly lies.

pages.text: Jordanian Jokesters On April 1, 2010, a newspaper in Jordan had an interesting front- page story. It reported that three spaceships had landed in the desert nearby. Some people in the town were not used to April Fools’ pranks and got scared. The newspaper apologized for the story. Sizdah Bedar The Iranian (Persian) calendar is very old. The thirteenth day of the Iranian new year is called Sizdah Bedar (seez-DAH be-DAR). It falls around April 1 and has been around since 536 bc. On Sizdah Bedar, families and friends share picnics, pranks, and fun. It might just be the oldest-known joke day in history. April Fools’ Day.
pages.brief: A Jordanian newspaper office prints a surprising front-page story about three spaceships landing in the nearby desert, while townspeople look frightened; in an Iranian park, families and friends share a picnic with playful pranks and fun.

pages.text: Famous Foolery Some April Fools’ jokes are famous. Spaghetti Trees? In 1957, a British TV show described a spaghetti tree. When the show was over, many people called the station wanting one.
pages.brief: In a 1957 British television studio, a presenter describes a spaghetti tree; afterward, many hopeful viewers crowd telephone lines calling the station, eager to ask for a spaghetti tree of their own and ask questions.

pages.text: Corporate Chaos Companies and the media fool people, too. On April 1, 1996, Taco Bell said that it had bought the American Liberty Bell. The company said it would now be called the “Taco Liberty Bell.” Many people believed the story. The company had to say it was a joke. In 1998, Burger King showed an ad for a left-handed burger. They said it made left-handed eating easier. April Fools’ Day.
pages.brief: In a Taco Bell office, company leaders announce a joke purchase of the American Liberty Bell and rename it; outside, customers react with surprise. Nearby, a Burger King advertisement shows a left-handed burger designed for easier eating.

pages.text: Online Pranks Internet April Fools’ jokes spread fast. One of Google’s famous jokes was a drink it said made people smarter. In 2012, a radio station said that Twitter was changing to 133 characters per tweet. It was a joke. In 2013, Twitter said it would ask people who used vowels in their tweets to pay more. This, too, was a joke. Even Pokémon Go began as an Internet joke in 2014. Google Maps said it had a tool that would find the best Pokémon Master in the world.
pages.brief: People gather around computers and phones as online jokes spread: a Google drink promises smarter users, a radio station announces a Twitter change, and a Google Maps tool claims to find the best Pokémon Master in the world.

pages.text: Conclusion Follow certain rules during April Fools’ Day. Don’t be mean. If you’re going to make a joke, make sure you can take a joke in return. Many places around the world enjoy April Fools’ Day. Keep it safe and fun! April Fools’ Day.
pages.brief: A group of friends from different places laugh together in a cheerful park after harmless April Fools’ jokes, showing they can take a joke in return; everyone stays safe and kind, with smiling faces and no one upset.

books.title: Itching and Scratching
books.art_why: Itching, skin, insects, and medicines are real-world subjects that can be photographed.

pages.text: Itching and Scratching.
pages.brief: A simple, plain background with a close-up of human skin and a hand scratching an itchy patch; the scene focuses only on the action of itching and scratching, with no other objects or people visible.

pages.text: Itching Scratching and.
pages.brief: A plain background with a close-up of a hand scratching bare skin; the hand pauses for a moment as the itch returns, showing the simple action of itching and scratching without any other objects or people.

pages.text: Tickle, Touch, Scratch It starts with a tickle. You brush your hand against your skin, but the tickle continues. You can’t help but scratch. Ahh, relief, but it lasts just a moment. Then the feeling returns, even stronger. Before long, you’re scratching away again. We’ve all had that experience. There are dozens of reasons for itching, and there’s a good explanation for why scratching seems to relieve an itch.
pages.brief: A close-up of a person’s hand brushing against the skin of their arm; the same hand scratches the itchy spot, showing a brief sense of relief before the urge to scratch returns again, even stronger.

pages.text: More Than Skin-Deep When you think of itching, you usually think of skin. It’s true that itching happens mostly on your skin. After all, skin covers your whole body. Skin is also the only thing that stands between the inside of your body and the outside world. All sorts of things touch your skin. Skin has nerve cells that react when something touches it. Some of those things are harmless. Some, however, are harmful or even dangerous. An itch is your body’s way of warning that these things can hurt you. For example, many people are allergic to poison ivy. This plant has irritating oils that rub off on skin. The oils make skin blister and ooze. Open blisters can get infected. The oils can also affect other parts of the body, like the nose and lungs. Contact with poison ivy can cause a bad infection to develop.
pages.brief: A close-up of human skin with tiny nerve cells reacting as something touches it; beside it, a poison ivy plant with oily leaves and a patch of blistered, oozing skin that can become infected.

pages.text: Your body uses itching to keep infections from happening. Itching is a signal from your immune system—your body’s internal system that helps protect you from sickness. When you touch poison ivy, your immune system triggers an itch. This informs you that your skin has touched something harmful. In this case, the itch teaches you to stay away from poison ivy. The Itch-Scratch Cycle.
pages.brief: A person stands beside a poison ivy plant and touches its leaves; a close-up shows red, itchy skin on the hand as the body’s immune system reacts, warning the person to stay away from the plant.

pages.text: Causes of Itching It’s not just your skin that itches. Your eyes can feel itchy, too, and so can your nose and throat. Scratching is a reflex action to itching—something you do automatically, or without thinking. However, you can’t reach down your throat to scratch it, so you cough. You can’t scratch inside your nose, so you sneeze. Scratching your eyes can cause damage, so you rub them instead. All those actions have the same goal: to remove whatever is causing the itch. Perhaps you ate something spicy. Maybe you breathed dust or got smoke in your eyes. A good cough, sneeze, or rub could get rid of the problem!
pages.brief: A person rubs itchy eyes, coughs with a hand near the throat, and sneezes; nearby, a bowl of spicy food, a dusty cloud, and smoke show possible causes that can make eyes, nose, and throat itch.

pages.text: Sometimes, though, you can’t get rid of the cause of your itch easily. Sometimes the cause comes from a germ inside your body. The itch you feel may be part of a sickness caused by the germ. Chicken pox is a sickness caused by a virus. The virus makes the skin break out in very itchy blisters. Today, many children get a vaccine to prevent them from getting chicken pox. Luckily, for those who do get sick, chicken pox is a temporary condition. After a while, the sickness passes.
pages.brief: A child’s skin covered in itchy chicken pox blisters; nearby, a vaccine vial and syringe represent the vaccine many children receive to prevent the sickness, and the blisters appear as a temporary condition that passes.

pages.text: There are other itchy conditions, though, that last much longer. These are known as chronic conditions. Some just affect the skin. Others cause different parts of the body to itch. One chronic condition, psoriasis, speeds up the life cycle of skin cells. The cells build up on the surface and form itchy scales. Another condition, eczema, is a rash that is common in children but can occur in people at any age. Chronic conditions have no cure. People who suffer from them can do some things to help, though. For instance, they can avoid using skin care products that may cause the condition to flare up.
pages.brief: A close-up of skin with itchy scales from psoriasis and a red eczema rash on a child’s arm; nearby, bottles of skin care products are set aside because they may cause the condition to flare up.

pages.text: Insect bites, especially mosquito bites, are another common cause of itching. Female mosquitos feast on blood. Their bites can introduce dangerous germs to your bloodstream. Mosquitos can spread serious diseases, such as malaria and dengue fever. Fortunately, their bite causes your body to itch almost immediately. The itch catches your attention and makes you swat the insect away to protect yourself from even more bites. In this case, an itch can be a real lifesaver!
pages.brief: A female mosquito lands on a person’s arm and bites, taking blood; the person quickly swats it away, and a red itchy bump rises on the skin almost immediately, showing how the itch protects from more bites.

pages.text: Nervous System People once thought that itching was a form of pain. It isn’t. It does have a relationship with pain, though. That relationship is why scratching helps relieve itching. Your body has a network of nerves that feel all sorts of sensations. Nerves that sense itching overlap with nerves that feel pain. Nerves can only sense one feeling at a time. Unlike itching, scratching is a form of pain. When you apply pain by scratching, coughing, or rubbing, the painful feeling blocks the itch. For some people, the pain is almost pleasant because it stops the misery of itching.
pages.brief: A close-up of skin with a network of nerves beneath it; a hand scratches the itchy spot, and the pain signal from scratching blocks the itch signal, leaving the person relieved as the misery stops.

pages.text: Too much scratching can cause problems. If you scratch until you bleed, you set yourself up for infection. Scratching blisters can leave scars. Constantly rubbing your eyes can hurt them. A coughing fit makes it hard to catch your breath. Creepy Crawlies One of the creepiest sources of itching is the mango fly of Africa. This insect may lay eggs on clothes hung out to dry. When the eggs hatch, the larvae burrow under the skin of the person wearing the infected clothes. The larvae cause serious itching until they mature and burst out from sores on the skin.
pages.brief: A person scratches until the skin bleeds and rubs sore eyes; nearby, clothes hang out to dry in Africa as a mango fly lays eggs, and larvae burrow under a person’s skin, causing itchy sores.

pages.text: Oh, What a Relief! Scratching temporarily relieves itching, but it’s not a good long-term solution. For chronic itching, you need lasting relief. The best solution, of course, is to remove the cause of the itch. Sometimes, though, that is not possible. Lotions and creams can offer some relief, and so can eyedrops. These are topical medicines, which means they are applied to the surface of the body. Topical medicines contain substances that soothe itches. Some people have even found relief by taking a bath in oatmeal!
pages.brief: A person applies soothing lotion to itchy skin and puts in eyedrops; a bathtub filled with an oatmeal bath sits nearby, showing topical medicines that soothe the itch when the cause cannot be removed easily.

pages.text: For severe itching, you may have to take oral medicines. These come in the form of pills, capsules, or liquids that you swallow. Oral medicines block or lessen your body’s response to whatever causes an itch. The urge to scratch goes away. Itchy Critters Animals scratch for many of the same reasons humans do. But there’s another reason that animals scratch: they need to molt. Molting means shedding fur, feathers, or skin as the animal grows or as the seasons change. Furry animals shed hair. Birds lose feathers. Reptiles such as snakes crawl out of their old skin. Scratching speeds the process along. Animals may rub against trees or rocks to get rid of their old layers.
pages.brief: A person swallows an oral medicine pill with water; nearby, a furry animal sheds hair, a bird loses feathers, and a snake crawls out of its old skin, rubbing against a rock to speed the molt.

pages.text: Itch, Scratch, Learn Feeling itchy isn’t fun, but think of it as a safety mechanism. It’s part of your body’s amazing defense system. Itching lets you know what is bad for you and teaches you to avoid it. The next time you feel itchy, ask yourself why—before you scratch. Learning what makes you itch and avoiding it is the best way to keep from getting itchy again! Things You Can Do If you have troublesome itching, there are some things you can do that may relieve it and prevent damage caused by scratching. These include: • patting or tapping the itchy area rather than scratching it. • holding a cold, damp cloth against the itchy area to cool it down. • washing in cool or lukewarm water. • using nonperfumed skin care products. • avoiding wearing clothes that irritate your skin, such as wool or polyester. • applying a cream to dry or flaky skin.
pages.brief: A person pats an itchy arm instead of scratching, holds a cold damp cloth against the skin, and washes in cool water; nearby are nonperfumed skin products, soft non-wool clothes, and cream for dry, flaky skin.

books.title: Treasure Found
books.art_why: Real treasure, divers, ships and museum objects exist today; this is not a biography of one famous person.

pages.text: TABLE OF CONTENTS.
pages.brief: A calm, open page with a simple decorative frame and small treasure-hunting motifs, suggesting the start of a book for young readers; no characters or scene are shown, and the mood is inviting and orderly.

pages.text: INTRODUCTION On Saturday morning, you are busy cleaning your room. Under your bed, you discover a box. You look inside. You see a plastic ring, a birthday card with a dollar inside, a shell, and a postcard from a friend. You say, “Wow! I forgot about this stuff.” You have just found treasure.
pages.brief: A young child kneels beside a bed in a tidy bedroom, holding an open box. Inside are a plastic ring, a birthday card with a dollar, a shell and a postcard. The child looks surprised and delighted.

pages.text: TREASURE HUNTING Treasure is anything that someone thinks is valuable. Over the years, much treasure has been found. In 1922, Howard Carter found gold and gems in the tomb of ancient Egypt’s King Tutankhamun. In 1874, Heinrich Schliemann dug up an ancient Greek city. In 1964, Robert Marx found a city, too, under the sea near the island of Jamaica. He also discovered thousands of silver coins.
pages.brief: A three-part scene shows Howard Carter beside gold and gems in an ancient Egyptian tomb, Heinrich Schliemann at an ancient Greek city dig, and Robert Marx underwater near Jamaica, finding a sunken city and thousands of silver coins.

pages.text: In Florida, Kip Wagner picked up some Spanish coins called “pieces of eight,” which had washed up on the shore. He knew they had come from a shipwreck. He started to search the ocean floor. He wanted to find the shipwreck. Over time, he found sunken treasure worth millions of dollars.
pages.brief: On a Florida shore, Kip Wagner bends to pick up Spanish coins called pieces of eight. He looks toward the ocean, then is shown underwater searching the seafloor near a shipwreck, with piles of sunken treasure worth millions nearby.

pages.text: SUNKEN TREASURE Sunken treasure is especially hard to find because it is under water. Yet, people continue to search for treasure deep under the sea. A Spanish ship called the Atocha (ah-TOH-cha) held one of the most famous sunken treasures. In 1622, a group of Spanish ships, including the Atocha, took on a cargo of gold, silver, coins, and gems. The ships left Havana, Cuba, headed for Spain. They sailed into the path of a great storm. The Atocha and several of the other ships in the group sank near the Florida Keys.
pages.brief: Under the sea, a Spanish ship called the Atocha lies broken near the Florida Keys. Above, the ship is shown leaving Havana, Cuba, loaded with gold, silver, coins and gems, then caught in a great storm before sinking.

pages.text: Spain sent ships to find the cargo from the sunken shipwrecks. Divers found the cannon from the Santa Margarita, one of the ships from the group. They could not find anything else because another storm had broken up that ship. They did not find any sign of the Atocha.
pages.brief: Divers search a sunken shipwreck and find a cannon from the Santa Margarita, one of the Spanish ships, after another storm has broken up that ship. Broken wreckage lies scattered around them, and the dark water shows no sign of the Atocha.

pages.text: MEL FISHER AND THE ATOCHA For years, people dreamed of finding the Atocha. Mel Fisher dreamed of it, too. As a boy, he had read Treasure Island, the story of a young man who went looking for pirate treasure. Mel wanted to find lost treasure. Luckily, he liked diving under the sea. He even owned a dive shop. In the early 1960s, Mel Fisher decided to look for the Atocha. Friends and family, including his wife, sons, and only daughter, joined in the search. People gave him money to help with the search. Everyone would share the treasure when the Atocha was found.
pages.brief: As a boy, Mel Fisher reads Treasure Island and dreams of lost treasure. Later, he stands in his dive shop and then plans the Atocha search with his wife, sons, daughter, friends and family, while supporters give money to help.

pages.text: For several years, Mel and his crew searched the ocean. They used metal detectors and sonar to find pieces of the ship on the seafloor. Sonar can find things deep under the water that cannot be seen. Mel and his crew found many things, including other shipwrecks, but not the Atocha. Do You Know? Sonar uses sound to find objects under the water. A sound wave is sent out. When it hits an object it bounces back to the sensor. The sonar echoes are used to form an image.
pages.brief: Mel Fisher and his crew search the ocean from a boat, using metal detectors and sonar. A sonar sound wave is shown bouncing off an object underwater and returning to a sensor to form an image. They find other shipwrecks, but not the Atocha.

pages.text: Florida GULF OF MEXICO Florida Florida Keys X MARKS THE SPOT In 1970, Mel and his crew got help from a friend named Eugene Lyon. He looked through old books about Spanish ships. In them, he read the Atocha ’s cargo list and clues to where the ship could be found. He told Mel that he had been looking in the wrong place!
pages.brief: Eugene Lyon studies old books about Spanish ships and reads the Atocha’s cargo list and location clues. Beside him, a map shows the Florida coast, the Gulf of Mexico and the Florida Keys, with a large X marking a new search area.

pages.text: Mel and his crew sailed one hundred miles from where they had been looking to a new place. Three years later, they found silver bars with markings they had not seen before. These markings matched the Atocha ’s cargo list. Now they knew they were near the treasure. Still, two years later, they had not found the ship. Then, tragedy struck. Mel’s son, Dirk; Dirk’s wife, Angel; and a diver, Rick Gage, drowned when their search boat overturned in the ocean.
pages.brief: Mel Fisher and his crew sail to a new search area. They hold silver bars whose markings match the Atocha’s cargo list. Later, grief fills the scene as a search boat overturns in the ocean, and Dirk, Angel and diver Rick Gage drown.

pages.text: Mel was saddened by the loss, but he decided to continue the search. For ten more years, he and his crew searched for the remains of the ship. In 1985, Mel and his crew finally found the cargo hold of the Atocha. The treasure included gold and silver worth millions of dollars. Mel and his crew marked where everything had been found. They took pictures, too. They wrote down information for historians who might want to study what happened to the ship.
pages.brief: An older Mel Fisher and his crew continue searching for ten more years. In 1985 they find the Atocha’s cargo hold, filled with gold and silver worth millions. They mark the spot, take pictures and write down information for historians.

pages.text: The treasure from the Atocha was great and very valuable. Mel gave a part of the treasure to the state of Florida. He also gave some of the treasure to museums. He shared the rest of the treasure with his family and others who had helped him in his search. He sold some of it, too. Today, you can visit the Mel Fisher Maritime Heritage Society and Museum in Florida. You can see many of the beautiful things he found.
pages.brief: Mel Fisher shares the Atocha treasure: some goes to the state of Florida, some to museums, and some to family and helpers; he sells the rest. Today, visitors look at beautiful gold and silver objects in the Mel Fisher Maritime Heritage Society and Museum in Florida.

pages.text: CONCLUSION What treasure still waits to be discovered? You could join one of the many treasure- hunting groups around the world. You might discover an ancient city or tomb, or even a sunken or buried chest of gold. You can find many books and websites about treasure and treasure hunting. Maybe you will be the one to find the next great treasure.
pages.brief: A young reader stands with a treasure-hunting group, looking toward an ancient city, a tomb, and a sunken or buried chest of gold. Books and websites about treasure lie nearby, suggesting the reader may find the next great treasure.
